The session begins.

The city is behind you now, only a smudge of smoke to the north. To the west the Sea of Swords has gone the colour of old pewter, and the sun is sliding toward it. Tamsin walks a half-step ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, talking about who on the quay owes whom, and the cat pads along the verge, tail up, stopping now and then to smell the gorse.

Then the road bends around a stand of wind-bent pines, and there is a wagon.

It is a small two-wheeled carter's cart, tipped at an angle, one wheel sunk in the ditch. The mule is still in harness. It lifts its head, looks at you without much interest, and goes back to the grass. Sacks are lashed down under a canvas. Nobody is on the seat, nobody is in the ditch, nobody is on the road as far as you can see, and beyond the bend the road can't be seen at all. Something small and pale lies on the seat, too far away to make out.

Tamsin stops. The cat has stopped too, ears forward, staring at the trees.

"Well," Tamsin says, already shrugging the pack a little lower, "nobody leaves a mule standing. Not on this road." She looks back at you. The light is going. The Friendly Arm is still somewhere ahead.

Party: Tamsin (HP 11/11) — A porter from the Baldur's Gate quay who has carried James's pack since the evening he arrived. She knows the quay and everyone on it, and she is reckless. She 
Place: The Coast Way, south of Baldur's Gate
Time: Day 1 · afternoon

James closes his fingers on Tamsin's sleeve and she stops mid-stride, half turned, with the pack swinging against her back. She looks at his hand, then at the cat, and keeps her mouth shut. For her that is a lot.

He moves off the road to the seaward side. The gorse is waist-high there, thick and full of thorns, and the soft boots make no sound on the turf. He crouches where the bushes thin enough to see through.

From here the cart is about eighty feet off. He reads the scene the way the scouts taught him in Tethyr, road first and trees second, and it doesn't take long.

The mule has grazed the verge bare in a rough circle as far as its traces reach. It has been standing there for hours, not minutes. The sunk wheel didn't skid in. The ruts run straight down the road and then turn hard into the ditch, as if someone hauled the mule's head round on purpose. In the mud beside the wheel there are boot-prints, and plenty of them. Most are big and broad, wider across the ball of the foot than any man's he has marched with, and pressed deep. Between them runs one smaller pair of a man's boots with worn heels, walking rather than dragged. The prints don't go back north. They cross the road and go into the pines, the big ones in front and behind and the small ones in the middle. Nobody else's prints come back out over them.

Nothing moves in the stand of trees. No branch is bent wrong, no light catches on metal, no bird has gone quiet. The pines just creak in the sea wind. Beyond them, a good way east and south, a single grey thread of smoke climbs out of the wood and leans inland. That's someone's fire, and nobody has a farm out there.

The pale thing on the seat is a flat piece of bone about the size of a palm, held down by a stone so the wind won't take it. Something is scratched into its face. At this distance it's only marks; he can't make out letters.

Pip hasn't moved from the verge. His ears are still forward, but his tail has dropped low and he's breathing through his open mouth. James feels a small push of sensation through the bond, no words: *many. sweat, iron, smoke. old smell, not now. that way.* The cat's whiskers point into the pines, along the prints.

Tamsin squats down next to James in the gorse, too close, so her shoulder bumps his.

"Walked it? No. I've never been past the wall before today," she says, low and fast. "Didn't I say? I didn't say. Doesn't matter. But I've heard it all on the quay, the carters never shut up. There's a stone bridge just past the bend where a brook comes down off the hills. Wood on the land side, that side, all the way down, thick, and the road runs right along it. To the Arm it's the rest of the evening at a walk, if they're not lying, and they always are. A dozen friends?" She glances at the prints by the wheel, then at the trees. "You could hide a hundred in there. And they've been saying since spring there's orcs on this stretch. Taking tolls. I thought that was drink talking." She swallows. "Those aren't drunk feet, are they."

The mule tears up another mouthful of grass. The sun touches the sea.

 (Out of game: none of these needed a roll. Stopping Tamsin and crouching in the gorse carry no risk, reading a road for an ambush is routine for an old Tethyrian scout, nobody is hiding in the pines to roll against, and from that distance the bone tally's marks can't be read, so all of it was told as it happened.)

Tamsin looks at the crossbow as if he'd handed her a live eel. Then she takes it the way she'd take a pole off a quay cart, both hands in the middle, until he turns the stock into her shoulder and lays her finger along the guard, clear of the trigger.

"Look like I might," she repeats quietly. "I can do that. I do it to the harbourmaster every day." She settles into the gorse with the pack against her knees and the bolt pointed more or less at the pines. Her mouth is still set hard.

James goes along the seaward verge, bent low. The gorse catches at his cloak but doesn't make a sound. Level with the cart, he waits for one breath, then crosses the open ruts in four quick steps and drops into the cart's shadow on the side away from the trees. The boots make no sound in the mud. The mule swings its head round, blows at him once and goes back to grazing.

Through the bond, Pip's attention sits at the back of his head like a hand on a shoulder. The cat is still on the verge with his nose to the pines. *Same. Old. Gone in.* The smell isn't getting any fresher.

James lifts the stone off the seat and tilts the bone to catch the last of the light.

It's a sheep's shoulder blade, scraped clean. The letters were cut with a knife point in a heavy, careful hand, the hand of someone who learned his letters late and doesn't like them. They're in Common:

**ODO FENNICK**

Under the name are thirty short strokes, bundled in fives with a slash through each bundle, and after them the word **GOLD**. Below that comes a line cut deeper than the rest, as if this was the part that mattered:

**WYRM ROCK — LT**

That's Wyrm's Rock, the Fist's fortress in the middle of the bridge. They walked under its walls just after noon. The *LT* is cut neatly and nothing follows it. It's no name, only a rank. Whoever cut this knew where the bone had to go and which kind of officer it went to.

He puts the bone back on the seat. Then he lifts a corner of the canvas.

The cart holds sacks of salt in coarse sacking, grey sea-salt crusted white along the seams where the damp has got in. He counts eight. Each one has the same mark stamped in black on its flank, a shape with spread wings, crude and blocky like a brand burned into a crate. The lashings across the back of the bed have been cut and knotted again, tidily. There's a pale square on the boards at the back where the wood hasn't weathered, and the rope is slack across it. Four sacks used to sit there, maybe five. Nothing else has been touched. The rest of the load is roped down as neatly as if the carter had done it himself. Whoever took the salt took a share and then tied the rest down for the next owner.

The wind comes in off the sea, steady and cold now that the sun has gone into the water. It carries a sound up the road from somewhere past the bend, where the land drops toward the brook. It's a laugh, deep, from a big chest, and it goes on a beat too long. Then another voice says something short, and then there's nothing but the wind in the pines.

Pip's ears turn from the trees to the road. *That way. New. Not in the trees. Ahead.*

 (Out of game: none of these four needed a roll. Spanning and loading a light crossbow is routine for an old soldier, and it happened before he handed it over: I should have shown it, and the bolt sits in the groove now. Feeling Pip's mood through the bond is part of the pact and isn't a check. Nobody was watching from the pines and his boots are silent, so there was no one to roll Stealth against. The bone is cut in plain Common letters, so up close he just reads it.)

Place: The Coast Way, south of Baldur's Gate · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

James's voice is barely louder than the gorse. Tamsin listens without looking away from the pines. At *bill of lading* one corner of her mouth goes tight.

"Thirty gold," she says. "For a salt carter. Ned— nobody on the quay clears thirty in a season." She stops there and shifts the crossbow so its weight rests on her knee and not against his ribs. "Hand on your arm. Hard. No shooting, no shouting." She breathes out through her nose. "Go on, then. I'll watch your sack of salt."

Pip has already gone. He drops off the verge into the gorse and is out of sight at once. For a while the only sign of him is the tops of the bushes moving, and then nothing moves at all. James counts slowly the way scouts count, gives him a good long while, and closes his eyes.

The world drops to a cat's height. It goes sharp and grey and very loud. Each stem of gorse stands out on its own. The sea is a roar off to the right. Under everything comes the brook, a quick chuckle of water over stones. Pip is lying flat under the last bush before the ground falls away. From there he moves forward one paw at a time.

The bush ends, and Pip doesn't stop. He drops down the bank on the land side of the road, into wet nettles at the foot of the bridge's near wall, where the stone meets the slope and the shadow is already black. Nothing up on the road turns his way. He follows the wall to its end and climbs, belly to the stone. He tucks himself into a crack between the last coping-block and the earth, close enough that the smell of them floods his nose: sweat, leather, iron, woodsmoke caught in hair, and meat eaten not long ago.

On James's own chest, somewhere far off in the body he has left in the gorse, the Lady's coin turns warm.

There are three of them on the bridge.

The nearest, about fifteen feet from the cat, is big even for an orc. He's broad through the shoulders and grey-green in the last light. He sits on the parapet with one boot up and a greataxe across his knees as if it weighs nothing. His hair is tied back with a thong. A second thong around his neck holds a heavy coin that hangs on his chest and catches what is left of the sky as silver. While the other two talk, he takes the coin off his chest without looking at it, flips it, and slaps it onto the back of his hand. He looks. He keeps looking a moment longer than a man looks at a coin he expected. Then he grunts, lets it fall back on its thong, and rubs his eyes with a thumb and finger.

*Big one. Tired. The iron one. Not near him.* The cat's dread of the axe comes down the bond as a flattening of the ears.

The second orc is younger and leaner, with a spear grounded beside him. He stands in the middle of the road, facing north toward the bend, telling the big one a story with his free hand. It's in Orcish, harsh and quick, and James doesn't have a word of it. At the end the young one laughs. It's the laugh they heard from the cart, deep and a beat too long. The big one doesn't laugh. He says one short word, and the young one shuts his mouth and looks north again. He's watching the road, not the gorse.

The third sits on the far parapet with his back half to the brook. He's working an edge onto a javelin head with a stone, and three more javelins lean against the wall beside him. He hasn't looked up once.

There's no fourth on the bridge. No man in worn-heeled boots, no prisoner, nobody tied. The road beyond runs on south into the dusk, empty.

Pip's nose goes down past the wall's edge, into the dark under the arch where the brook runs. *Under. Salt. Sacking. Dug earth, new.* After a breath comes something more puzzled: *Man smell not here. Man went the other way. Trees.* That's the way the prints went from the cart, east, toward the smoke.

Back in the gorse no hand closes on James's arm. Tamsin's shoulder stays where it was against his, warm and still. For the moment, all the wind brings him from his own side is the cat's world.

The young orc shifts his spear to the other hand and keeps watching the bend. The sky over the sea is going from pewter to slate. In a little while it will be too dark for anyone on the road without an orc's eyes.

 (Out of game: all three happened in the turn. Pip's creep to the bridge was rolled as his Stealth check, a natural 20, so he got within fifteen feet unseen. Posting Tamsin as lookout and looking through Pip's senses carry no risk and are part of the pact, so neither needed a roll.)

The weight of the cat's senses lifts off him and he's back in his own body: cold face, gorse thorns at his knee, Tamsin's shoulder warm against his. The sea is louder from here. Down the bond he feels Pip take the order. The cat doesn't answer in words, just a flick of his attention as he turns around in the crack and starts down the wall.

Pip comes back the way he went: down into the nettles, along the foot of the wall, up the bank. Nobody on the bridge turns his way. The young orc keeps watching the bend and the whetstone keeps scraping. A while later the gorse beside James shivers and the cat pushes in under his elbow. His coat is wet from the nettles and he smells of the brook. He sits down and starts washing a paw as if he'd only been out to the end of the garden.

Tamsin hears the count without interrupting. When he gets to *buried the salt under the arch* her eyebrows go up. When he says *the man went east* she looks at the smoke, and she keeps looking at it while he gets to the part about her.

She doesn't answer right away. She shifts the crossbow on her knee, finger still along the guard where he put it.

"Stand behind you. Hold this. Do nothing else," she says, low, like a list being checked off. Then, in her ordinary quick voice: "Yes. I can. I've stood behind the harbourmaster while he told a Calishite captain his berth fee had doubled, and I kept my face. This is the same, only bigger and greener."

She chews her lip.

"But listen, about the mule. You walk up there with their mule and their cart, that's not *a traveller*. That's someone who's been to the cart and read the bone. They left that bone for somebody to carry north. Fine, maybe that's who you want to be. But a man who stopped to read a ransom and still walks up and asks the toll? On the quay, a man who walks up already knowing the price is either a buyer or trouble, and they'll look at you the way you'd look at either." She lifts one shoulder. "So which is he? The one in the other face. Is he buying the carter back, or does he just want to know the price?"

The sky over the water has gone from slate to ink at the bottom edge. On the bridge, where they can't see it, the whetstone has stopped.

Tamsin hears him out with her head on one side. At *factor* she nods once, the way she'd nod at a fair price on the quay.

"Blackwing," she says. "The wings. It's Blackwing Salts, the chandlery off Gray Harbor. Half the inns on the Way buy from them. If you're their man, you're sour, you're tight with money, and you think orcs are a line in the ledger." One corner of her mouth twitches. "I've carried for their factors. I know the face."

Then his face stops being his. The mask settles over him the way a coat does. He's heavier in the jaw and softer under the chin, and his hair has gone grey at the temples. The grey infantry cloak hangs as good brown wool with a strip of fur at the collar, and the rod is a walking stick with a brass knob. Tamsin looks him up and down and breathes out through her nose.

"Oh, that's horrible," she whispers. "That's exactly him."

Pip goes off into the gorse toward the bend without a sound, low and fast, and his attention settles at the back of James's head again.

The mule doesn't object to being led. It does object to the ditch. When James takes the headstall and asks it to walk on, it leans into the collar and the sunk wheel doesn't move. Tamsin lays the crossbow in the grass with the bolt still in it, gets her shoulder under the tailboard and says "*Hup*" the way she must say it a hundred times a day on the quay. Mule and porter heave together and the wheel comes out of the mud with a sucking lurch. She picks the crossbow up again, wipes her hands on her trousers and falls in a pace behind him on his left.

They go round the bend. The road drops toward the brook, and the bridge is there: low grey stone, the water loud under it, and three dark shapes against a sky that has almost no colour left. The young one sees them first. Of course he does. He has been watching this bend for hours, and in this light his eyes are better than theirs.

He shouts something in Orcish and brings the spear up level.

Down the bond, sharp and sudden: *Up. The thrower is up. One in his hand.* Through the cat's eyes, low among the nettles at the bridge end, James sees the javelin orc on his feet on the far parapet. His arm is cocked and ready but he hasn't thrown.

The big one doesn't stand at first. He turns his head, looks at the cart, at the mule and at the fat man in the fur collar, and only then gets off the parapet. The greataxe comes with him in one hand, head down, the way a man carries a tool.

Forty feet out, James plants the stick and calls across the water noise in the voice of a man who has been put out all day.

Ushkar listens all the way to the end. He looks at the fur collar, the fat hands, the brass-knobbed stick, and the quay girl behind with the crossbow and the sour face. For a moment he looks at James the way James has watched men look at a dealer they've decided is honest. Then he stops thinking about whether the factor is real and starts thinking about the factor's money.

He says one word in Orcish without turning his head. The young one's spearpoint drops to the road. On the far parapet the javelin goes down to rest against the stone. *Down,* Pip reports. *Still holding it.*

Then the big orc does something James didn't expect. He walks off the bridge toward them alone and leaves the other two behind. He stops ten feet off, close enough that the brook covers his voice from his own men, and rests the axe head on the road.

This close, James's own eyes can do what the cat's did. The silver on the thong is the size of a big man's thumbnail and too heavy to be any coin of the Gate. On the face turned outward, worn soft by handling, is a woman's profile smiling at nothing. Under the merchant's coat, the Lady's coin on James's chest goes from warm to hot for the space of a breath, like a hand laid flat on his breastbone, and then it's only warm again.

"Salt man," the orc says. His Common is low and heavy. Every word sounds like something he has paid for. "Bill is not for you. Bill goes to the Rock. They pay." He tips his chin at the mule. "Mule, take. Is why we leave it. Cart goes north, bone goes with it." He looks past James at Tamsin and her crossbow for exactly as long as it takes to dismiss them both, then back again. "Your man is in the trees. Dry. Fed. Nobody hit him."

He waits. Behind him, the young one has started edging closer to hear, and the big one doesn't look round. He only lowers his voice further.

"You carry gold, salt man? Here?" One heavy finger taps the silver on his chest, and he doesn't flip it. "Thirty. In my hand, not to the Rock. Then he walks out of trees tonight, not in three days."

*(Out of game: that was a natural 20 on the Deception check, so the Lady's Heroic Inspiration is yours to spend on a reroll later.)*

 The lie works completely. The voice, the face, the impatience and the bill he wants settled all hang together without a seam, and the big orc takes James for exactly who he claims to be: Blackwing Salts' factor, come south in person to buy back his carter. From here on he's bargaining with a salt man, not sizing up a stranger. For a moment, somewhere at the back of James's head, there's the feeling of a card turned face up that he never had to play.

He takes the deal. He listens to the end, breathes out through his nose, and nods once, the way a man nods at a price he'd have asked for himself if he'd thought of it.

"Twenty," he says. "In my hand. He walks out first. You see boots, you hear name." He glances down at the merchant's stick and the man's sore feet, and something close to amusement crosses his face. "Is how it's done."

The young one, back on the road, gets nothing for his trouble. The brook takes every word. He gives up and stands there scowling at Tamsin's crossbow. Tamsin scowls straight back at him like she's been paid to.

At the question about the coin, the big orc's hand goes to the thong. He takes the silver off his chest without looking, thumbs it up, catches it and slaps it onto the back of his other hand in one movement he must have made a thousand times. He lifts his palm.

It hasn't landed on the Lady. The face turned up is the other side, and the other side is wrong. Somebody has scraped it flat and cut into it with a knife point or an awl, by hand and without much skill. It shows a single eye, wide open, with a few hard lines for lashes and a gouged dot for the pupil. Nobody would strike that into a coin's die. It looks up at the dusk, and under the merchant's coat James's own coin goes warm against his breastbone and stays warm.

The orc looks at it a moment longer than a man looks at a coin, the same as on the bridge. Then he closes his fist on it.

Tamsin hears the answer about the docket without looking at him. She turns the last of her crust over in her fingers.

The ale mug is pewter, dented and dull. Tilted on the bench at the right angle, its side gives James a smeared, curved picture of the hearth: a blot of dark coat, a pale face, and the pale square of the cup standing full beside it. That's not enough to read a man by. It is enough to see the coat shift each time cold air comes through the postern. A carter goes out to piss, and the coat shifts. The carter comes back, and it shifts again, then settles.

Tamsin listens to the errand with her eyes on the room.

"Pack's under my boots," she says out of the corner of her mouth. "Not on the cart. You're tired." She doesn't make anything of it. "I'll say I'm seeing Odo's mule got its water. Nobody asks a porter why she's looking at a mule." Under her breath: "Grey. Saddled or bedded. How many in today. Don't talk." She swings her boots down off the pack.

She's halfway up when he says the last thing, quietly.

She stops. For a moment her face isn't doing anything at all. It isn't the quay face or the dull face, and that's rarer on Tamsin than either of them. She looks down at him, then at the postern.

"Noted," she says, the way a clerk says it to close a line. Then she goes.

In the mug's dented side the dark coat turns its head as she crosses the room, and keeps it turned until the postern swings shut behind her.

James finishes the stew and wipes the bowl with the last of the bread. The fiddler gets through the slow tune and starts it again. By the hearth the old man has his pipe lit at last and puffs at it, pleased with himself. At the bar the young drover is telling Fenwick that it was a good hand, a *really* good hand. Fenwick says, "I'm sure it was," and wipes a mug at him in sympathy. Through the hatch comes the clatter of a ladle on iron and a woman's voice rising over the kitchen noise, too muffled to make out. It may be Margery Thorne getting the story out of a carter.

Tamsin is gone for about as long as it takes to water a mule. When the postern opens again she comes in rubbing her hands against the cold. In the pewter the dark coat follows her across the room, the way it did when she left. Then, for the first time in a while, it turns toward the corner bench.

She drops back onto her end of the bench, puts her boots up, takes the heel of her own bread off the plate and talks round it, bored, like someone passing on who's sleeping with whom.

"Mule's got water. Odo'd done it already, course he had." She chews. "Stable's down the side, past the kitchen door. Lad's asleep in the straw by the lamp, didn't wake him. Seven horses. Three in today with road mud still wet on the legs, cobs, same brand on the rump as the patch on that lot's sleeves." She tips her chin a hair toward the dicing guards. "Three with dry coats, been there days. And the grey."

She takes another bite before she gives him the rest.

"Grey's bedded. Rubbed down, rug on, hay in the net, the lot. He's not standing ready." She swallows. "But his saddle's not in the tack room with the others. Everybody else's tack is on the pegs inside. His is on his own stall door, bags still buckled to it, bridle hung on the post right by his head. You could have him tacked up in the time it takes to say it." She shrugs. "On the quay, a man who leaves his hook on the cart instead of the hut means to be first on tomorrow's load. Or he just doesn't trust the hut." She licks a crumb off her thumb. "Could be either. He did say early."

In the pewter the pale face is still turned toward the stair. Then it turns away. A hand comes up and lifts the wine, and for the first time since Fenwick poured it, Master Morrow drinks.

Out past the postern the bell hasn't rung yet. It's about ten minutes off, and nothing else happens before then unless you want it to.

I put a hand out and catch Tamsin's sleeve before she takes another step.

"Wait. Nobody leaves a mule standing — which is exactly why we stand here a moment first." I keep my voice low and nod at the cat. "He's not looking at the cart. He's looking at the trees."

I don't go to the wagon. I step off the road to the seaward side, where the gorse gives a little cover, and crouch, scanning the stand of pines and the ditch along it — anything moving, anything that doesn't belong, boot-prints in the mud by the sunk wheel. And I try to make out what the pale thing on the seat is from here, before anyone walks into whatever this is.

"Tamsin — you've walked this road. How far to the Arm from the bend, and is there anywhere between here and there a man could hide a dozen friends?"

"No," I say. "They're not."

I look at the sun, then at the smoke, and make the arithmetic a soldier makes: hours since they took him, one fire, no watch left on the cart. They've been and gone and they don't expect anyone to come down this road before dark.

"Stay here. Right here, in the gorse — if anything comes out of those trees that isn't me, you go north and you don't stop for the pack." I unhook the crossbow, span it, lay a bolt in the groove, and hand it to her. "Point this at them. You don't have to hit anything, you just have to look like you might."

Then I go to the cart. Not down the road — along the seaward verge, keeping low in the gorse until I'm level with it, then across quick and quiet in the soft boots, coming at it from the side away from the pines so the cart's bed is between me and the trees. I want the bone first: I lift the stone and read what's scratched on it. Then one look under the canvas to see what the sacks are, and whether anything has been taken from them.

And I keep one ear open through Pip the whole time — not his eyes, just whether that smell gets any newer.

I ease the canvas down and leave everything as it was — the stone back on the bone, the mark cut toward the road for whoever comes next. Then I go back the way I came, along the seaward verge, low and quiet, and drop into the gorse beside Tamsin.

"Toll orcs," I tell her, barely above the wind. "They've taken the carter. Odo Fennick. Thirty gold to a lieutenant at Wyrm's Rock, and they wrote it down like a bill of lading. That's not a raid, that's a business." I nod toward the bend. "And some of them are still on the road ahead. By the bridge, I'd guess. Laughing."

I crouch so my shoulder's against hers and the crossbow's between us. "I'm going to send the cat to look. While he's looking I can't see or hear a thing — I'll be sitting here like a sack of salt. So you're my eyes for a minute. Anything comes near us, you put your hand on my arm. Hard. Don't shoot, don't shout. Just grip."

Then I look at Pip and push the thought down the bond: *the bridge. Along the verge, in the gorse, not the road. Count them. Look for the man with the worn heels. Don't be seen.*

I let him go, give him time to get well down toward the bend, and then I close my own eyes and look through his.

I let go of the cat's eyes and the world comes back the right size — the cold on my face, Tamsin's shoulder, the wind. I breathe once and push down the bond, gentle: *good. Enough. Come back, same way.*

Then, to Tamsin, barely moving my lips: "Three. On the bridge, not in the trees. A big one with a greataxe who's seen a few winters, a young one with a spear watching the road north — that's our laugher — and one with javelins who hasn't looked up from his whetstone. No carter. They've buried the salt under the arch and the man went east, into the wood, toward that fire."

I rub my thumb over the coin on my chest. It's still warm.

"The big one flips a coin. Keeps looking at it like it's giving him an answer he doesn't like." I'm quiet a moment. "Tamsin, I want you to hear this plain, because I know what you'd do and I'd rather you didn't. Three orcs is a fight I can win from eighty feet if the dice fall right, and a fight that kills us both if they don't — the one with the javelins would have you before you'd finished looking brave. So I'm not going to start one. Not in the dark, not with the carter out of reach.

"Here's what I'm turning over. They're not raiders, they're tollmen. Tollmen talk. A traveller walks up to the bridge in the last light with a porter and a mule he found standing in the road, and asks what the toll is. That traveller doesn't have to be me — I can wear another man's face. What I want out of it isn't the bridge. It's where Odo Fennick is and what they'll take for him, from the mouth of the one who flips the coin." I look at her. "And you'd be standing behind me the whole time with that crossbow and your harbourmaster face. Can you do that and not do anything else?"

"Buyer," I say. "You're right, and it's a good catch. A traveller is wrong. A man who reads the bone and walks on is either a fool or the Fist, and I don't want to be either tonight."

I get my feet under me. "There was a mark on the sacks. Wings, black, stamped like a brand. That's somebody's salt house. So the man who walks up to the bridge is the salt house's factor — the fellow who signs for the carter's wages. Odo didn't come back, the factor rode south to find out why, found his cart in the ditch with a bill on the seat, and now he wants his mule, his man and the balance of his salt, and he's irritated about the price. That man is allowed to know the carter's name. He's allowed to be short with them. He's *expected* to haggle." I glance at her. "And a factor doesn't walk alone. He brings a hand off the quay who looks like she'd enjoy it if someone said no."

I take the Lady's coin between finger and thumb a moment. Still warm. The big orc flipping his own silver — I file that away.

Then I let the mask go on. Mask of Many Faces: a softer, older face than mine, forty-odd, clean-shaven, with the jowls of a man who eats at other people's expense; the cloak becomes a good brown merchant's coat with a bit of fur at the collar; the rod in my hand reads as a walking stick with a brass knob. I keep my own boots.

"Pip — stay in the gorse. Watch the javelin-man. If he stands up with one in his hand, I want to feel it."

I go back along the verge to the cart, take the mule's headstall, and talk to it until it decides I'm a person worth following. Then the three of us go round the bend onto the open road and toward the bridge at a walk, the cart creaking behind, Tamsin a pace back on my left with the crossbow carried low and loaded. Forty feet out, where the young one can see me plain, I stop, plant the stick, and call out in the voice of a man who has been inconvenienced all day:

"Evening. I'm looking for whoever wrote me a bill for thirty gold. I'll talk to him and no one else — and I'll have my mule back first, since nobody charged me for the loan of it."

[Onward]

I look at the silver on his chest a beat too long for a salt factor, and then make myself look at his face instead.

"Thirty was the Rock's price," I say, sour. "The Rock gets a lieutenant's wage and does nothing for it. You're the one who's fed my man for a day and kept your boys off him. So you and I can do better than thirty." I let the stick take my weight like a man whose feet hurt. "Twenty, in your hand, tonight. And I don't pay for a story about a dry man in the trees. He walks out onto this road where I can see his worn-out boots and hear him say his own name, then the purse crosses. That's how it's done on the quay, and I expect it's how it's done here."

I tap the brass knob once against the road, as if closing a ledger. "And the salt under your arch stays under your arch. I'm not sending a girl down a brook in the dark for four sacks. Call it your fee for the mule's grazing."

Then, quieter, almost offhand, the way you'd ask a man about his dog: "That coin. It's not Gate silver. Where does a man come by a piece like that?"
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I don't flinch from the axe. A factor who's made this trip has seen axes before. I look at it, then at him, with the tired contempt of a man asked a stupid question at the end of a long day.

"Who told me? Your knots told me." I point the stick back up the road, toward the bend. "I stood at that cart and counted eight sacks where there should be twelve. Lashings cut and tied again, neat as a chandler's boy. So four sacks of wet sea-salt went somewhere — and not into the trees. Nobody carries a hundredweight of salt a mile into a wood to feed a prisoner. You're tollmen. Tollmen keep the take close, and dry, and out of sight of the road." I shrug one heavy shoulder. "There's a bridge. There's an arch. I've been buying and losing salt on this coast for twenty years; where else would it be? If I'd said the trees you'd be laughing at me now."

I let the stick rest again, and lower my voice to match his. "I didn't come for salt. Salt is cheap and the sea makes more. I came for the man who drives it, because carters who know the road are not cheap. Keep your arch. Fetch my man."

Behind the merchant's face, I keep one small part of me on the bond — whether the javelin comes up again — and one part on the silver against his chest, going warm under my coat.

[Onward]

I turn half away from him, the way a careful man does when he opens a purse near strangers, and count twenty gold out of the fat purse under my coat into a separate kerchief — slowly, aloud under my breath, so he can hear the clink and the count and see that the rest goes back where it came from. I knot the kerchief and hold it in my fist, not offered yet.

Then, because a factor waiting on a bridge in the dark is a man who talks to fill the silence, and because this is the thing I actually want:

"Three days, you said. If the bone goes to the Rock." I make a face. "I've paid that lieutenant's toll before and never got a man back for it. You ride up to Wyrm's Rock with a bill like that, you ask for the LT, and what — some sergeant takes your gold and says come back Tenthday? I'd like to know the name of the man who's been eating my wages, since I'm about to stop paying him." I tip my head at him, merchant to merchant. "Who is he? And what's his cut of your thirty?"

"Then one of us is being robbed," I say, "and it isn't you, because you count what comes back." I turn the kerchief over in my fist. "You say the Rock isn't your choosing. I believe you. Nobody who takes tolls on a brook chooses to split them with a fortress. So somebody chose it for you — somebody who came down this road in spring, say, and told you where the bones go and what to cut on them." I nod at the thong at his neck without looking at the coin. "I don't ask who, because you've told me you don't know the lieutenant's name and I'd be a fool to ask what you'll say next. I ask this instead, merchant to merchant: when the thirty comes back from the Rock, who carries it? A Fist rider? A boy? Does it come as coin — or as a letter telling you what the next price will be?"

I shift my weight on the stick and look east, toward the dark where the spearman went. "And I'll take your offer. Next carter I lose, I come to you. But understand what you've just told me: if your bones all come home and mine didn't, then it wasn't your bone that got sent. Somebody's cutting their own, in your hand, for a different lieutenant. You might ask yourself how many carters you've been blamed for that you never took."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I give him the look of a man who's been asked to remember a ledger line from months back, and takes his time about it.

"Bran Tulley. Late spring — just after the Greengrass fairs. Not here." I shake my head and point the stick south, past the bridge, into the dark. "Past the Arm. The long empty stretch toward Beregost, where the Way runs by the hills and there's no brook and no bridge. His cart came back north with a Fist patrol — empty, no mule — and a bone on the seat like yours. Only I never held it. The Rock held it. A sergeant read it to me across a table and took my thirty and told me to come back. I came back twice. Then I stopped coming." I let my mouth go sour. "Tulley had a wife in Rivington. She still asks me."

I let that stand a moment, then lower my voice. "So if that's not your road and not your bone — then somebody south of here has learned your hand and your lieutenant both. I'd want to know that too."

I shift the stick and turn my head east, toward the pines, the way a nervous merchant does when he hears a wood go quiet — because Pip has just told me there are a lot of feet coming, and one spearman shouldn't need company to bring back one carter.

"That's more than one man coming through your trees," I say, flatly. "I paid for one."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I don't give him the half-breath he needs to finish that frown.

"Don't stand there gawping at me, Fennick," I snap across the water, in the voice of a man who has been inconvenienced since dawn. "No, you don't know me. Master Hallam's laid up with his gout and couldn't ride, so the house sent me, and you can thank him later that it sent anyone at all for a man who put eight sacks of good salt in a ditch." I jerk the stick at the cart. "Your mule's there. Walk to it. Now."

Then I turn to Ushkar, hold the kerchief out at arm's length — not stepping closer — and keep my eyes on his, not on the three spears or the thrower on the parapet.

"Twenty. Boots, name, as agreed. He walks past me, you take this, and your boys go back in the trees. That was the price, and you count what comes back." Lower, just for him: "Your young one brought three to a deal for one. I'd remember that, if I were the man who gives the orders here."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I don't argue. A factor who's paid his twenty doesn't want a ransom note lying about with his house's name on the cart it came off.

"Tamsin. The bone off the seat. Bring it here." I say it over my shoulder without turning, and I keep my eyes on him while she goes — the stick planted, the fur collar up against the wind off the brook, patient the way a man is patient when the business is nearly done.

When she puts it in my hand I weigh it a moment, then hold it out to him the way I held the kerchief, at arm's length, and let him take the two steps.

"It's yours. Burn it, drop it in the brook, I don't care — only don't let it go north. If the Rock asks why a carter walked in free, let them come down and ask you." I lower my voice to the register we've been using. "One more thing between merchants, and then I take my man home. That rider with the bright silver. Next time he puts a sack on your parapet — look at his horse's shoes, and look at his hands. A man who never spends his silver and never wears a coat is a man somebody is paying to be nobody. I'd like to know whose nobody he is. If you learn it, Blackwing Salts buys from the Friendly Arm, and the Arm buys from the road. Word finds me."

Then I turn my back on him — slowly, the way a man does who has decided to trust an axe — and walk to the cart, to Odo and the mule and the road north.

"Down," I say, loud enough to carry. "I didn't ride all this way to carry salt back to the sea. The Arm's paid half; the Arm gets its barrels. Walk her on, and keep her to the middle of the bridge."

Then quieter, for Odo alone, as I fall in beside the mule's head: "And keep your mouth shut till the water's behind us. All of it. I'll explain the rest when we can't be heard."

I push down the bond: *Pip. Stay low. Come once we're over.*

We cross as a factor crosses — the carter leading, the cart creaking, Tamsin a pace behind me with the crossbow carried low, me in the middle with the stick, not hurrying and not looking at the thrower. As we pass Ushkar on the parapet I give him the one civil nod a merchant gives a man he's just settled with, and nothing more.

Once the bridge is a dark shape behind us and the brook is only a sound, I let my shoulders come down a little, and ask Odo, low, without breaking stride: "Now. The camp. How many were there, really? Who gave the orders — the big one, or somebody else? And did anyone come to that fire today who wasn't an orc?"

"No," I say. "The four sacks aren't on you. Nor's the ditch. Twenty years says you don't put a cart in a ditch, and I believe twenty years."

I walk a few more paces, then stop the mule with a hand on the headstall, so the three of us stand together in the dark with the cart between us and the wind.

"Odo. Listen, because you've got maybe a quarter-hour to get used to this before you see it with your own eyes." I keep my voice level and low. "There is no Master Hallam, and there's no gout, and Blackwing Salts didn't send anyone. I'm not your factor. I'm a traveller who found your cart standing in the road with a bill on the seat, and I didn't like the arithmetic, so I borrowed a face that could pay it. This girl's a porter off the quay who's carried your house's salt and knew what your factors look like. That's all we are."

I let the mask go. The brown coat is a grey soldier's cloak again, the stick is a dark rod with a silver coin set in it, and the soft jowls are a leaner, younger face with a scout's eyes. I let him look.

"James Worgen. The twenty gold was mine, and I'm not asking you or Blackwing for it back. What I am asking is this. When you get to the Arm, you'll tell the story — you'd be no carter if you didn't. Tell it true. But tell it the way it was: the orcs fed you and never tied you and took thirty-odd gold for a bill to Wyrm's Rock. Don't make the big one a monster he wasn't and don't make me a hero I wasn't. Somewhere between that bridge and that fortress there's a lieutenant eating carters' wages, and I'd like the story to reach him in a shape that makes him nervous."

I nod at the mule. "Now walk her on. The Arm's kitchen wants its salt, and I want a chair by a fire where nobody's holding a javelin."

I let the cart roll on a dozen paces before I fall in beside Odo again, and this time I'm not a factor and not anyone's master — just a man walking beside a mule in the dark. I get the lantern out of my pack and hang it from the cart's tail-hook, lit low, so the Arm sees honest carters coming and not shadows.

"Wenna'll hear you're whole before she hears you were taken, if you walk fast enough. That's worth more than twenty gold, so call us square." I don't give him room to argue it.

Then, as we climb, I turn the Lady's coin over on its cord under my cloak, and think about the other one: a woman going south alone in spring, with no gold, who paid a toll with a piece of silver that lands how it likes and has an eye cut into its back. The coin on my chest went hot when it saw its sister. I don't say any of that aloud.

What I say is to Tamsin, low. "That rider. Bright new silver, not a scratch, never spent. You know the quay. Where does coin like that come from in the Gate — who handles money nobody's touched? The Counting House? A patriar's strongroom? Because whoever's paying thirty gold a carter to look like a lieutenant isn't paying it out of a soldier's wages."

And to Odo: "The Arm. Who's behind the bar there who hears everything and forgets nothing? When you tell your story tonight, I want to know whose ears it's falling on."

"A torch, then. Honest fire for honest carters." I take one from Tamsin's pack, light it from her tinderbox, wedge it in the tail-hook and knock it down to a low glow — enough that the Arm's gate sees a cart with a lamp, not three shadows coming out of the orc miles.

Then I walk a while without talking, and when I do it's to both of them.

"Here's how we come in at the gate. Odo, you're the carter you've always been, a day late with a reason. Corporal Strake asks, you tell her — all of it, the ditch, the fire, the bone, the thirty gold cut for a lieutenant at Wyrm's Rock. Don't soften that last part. Say the words 'Wyrm's Rock' plain and then stop talking and let her write." I glance at him. "I want to see what her pen does when it hears them. A corporal who writes every cart into a book has a book that could tell us how many carters on this road came home and how many didn't. I'd like to be the sort of man she lets read it, and the first step is being the man standing quietly behind an honest carter while he tells the truth.

"Tamsin — you're what you are. A porter who came south with a traveller. If anyone asks what I did, I found a cart in the road and paid a toll. That's true, and it's dull, and dull is what I want to be tonight. The sour fat man stays in the ditch."

And then, because it's been sitting under my cloak since the bridge: "Odo — twenty years on this road. Did you ever hear tell, back in spring, of a woman going south on foot, alone, no money? Paid Ushkar's toll with a coin instead of gold. He kept it. He still looks at it like it owes him an answer."

I pull a fresh torch from Tamsin's pack and light it off the stub before it dies, swap them in the tail-hook, and grind the old one out under my boot. Honest carters don't arrive in the dark.

Then I shift the rod to my belt, where it reads as nothing much, and fall in behind the cart on the off side — the traveller walking with the salt, not the man leading it. The crossbow I take back from Tamsin and sling across my own shoulder, unloaded, the bolt back in the quiver. A porter with a loaded crossbow is a question; a traveller with a slung one is furniture.

"Odo, she's yours," I say low. "Walk her up to the table like you've done a hundred times. Day late, with a reason. Tell it, say the words, look at the mule."

I keep a little behind and to the side where the gate lantern falls on Odo and the sacks and only half on me, and I watch Corporal Strake's hands — the pen, the page, whether she turns back to find his name from last month or writes him fresh — and I say nothing at all unless she asks me something directly.

To Pip, down the bond: *stay with the wheel. You're a cart cat.*

I step the rest of the way into the lantern light so she can see all of me, and take my hand well away from the rod at my belt before I speak. I don't take the cap off — I'm not a carter — but I stand the way you stand in front of a corporal who's writing things down, because I was infantry once and the body remembers.

"James Worgen. Late of Queen Zaranda's foot, in Tethyr, scouts after that. Walking to the Arm for work, same as half the men inside." I nod at the cart. "I found it standing in the road an hour before the bridge, with the mule grazing and the bone on the seat. I counted the prints and I counted the sacks, and I did the sum you just did — three days, a sister in Rivington selling her bed, and thirty gold landing in a pocket at Wyrm's Rock that nobody's name is on. I didn't like the sum. I had twenty, the orc wanted a deal more than he wanted a fortress, and the carter was a mile away through the trees. So I paid it."

I let that stand, then add the part she's really asking. "Why not leave it to the Fist? Corporal, I've carried a pay slip for an army. I know what a lieutenant earns. Thirty gold a carter, every one coming home neat in three days, with new silver nobody's spent — that's not a soldier's toll. That's somebody wearing a rank like I wore a fat man's face tonight." I glance at the margin of her book, at the slanted tick with no figure after it, then back to her eyes. "You write every cart in. You know how many of those ticks there've been since spring better than anyone on this road. I'd be glad to tell you everything the orc told me, in order, with no bread in it — and gladder if you'd tell me what number usually goes after that mark."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

"Mine," I say. "When I sit down it'll be the one you're looking at now. The other one's in a ditch by the brook and he isn't coming out." I give her the nod a soldier gives a corporal — not a salute, I'm not hers — and step back out of her light.

"Corner bench under the stair, at the bell. I'll be the one on it."

Then, to Odo, low as the cart starts to roll toward the side of the keep: "Kitchen. Tell Margery Thorne the salt's a day late because of orcs and the carter's whole because of nobody in particular. If she asks who paid, say a traveller, and let her come and find me if she wants the rest." I put a hand on the mule's neck a moment where his has been all day. "Go on. You're early."

And to Tamsin, as we go in through the postern and the fiddle and the dog-smell and the heat of a common room hit us like a wall: "Dull. Find us the corner bench and sit on it like you own it. I'll get us bread and whatever they're pouring, and we'll see who in this room looks up when a Blackwing cart comes in a day late with a strange man walking beside it."

I let Pip jump down and go wherever a cart cat goes, and I walk to the bar.

I put a silver on the bar, which is more than two stews and two ales come to, and don't ask for the change back yet.

"Two of the mutton, two of the plain ale. The good cider can stay a secret." I keep my voice easy and a little tired, the voice of a man with nothing to tell. "My bridge story's the dullest one you'll hear tonight, lad. Found a salt cart in the road with its mule grazing. Walked it down to the bridge. Three orcs wanted a toll. I paid it, they let us by. That's the whole of it." I shrug. "Carter's round at your kitchen door now, if Margery wants it from him. He tells it better. He was there longer."

I let him see me not looking at the card table — which takes doing, because I've already seen it. The thumb along the bottom edge before every deal: a man who wants to know where the last card sits. I've done it myself, years back, on worse nights than this. The Lady's coin lies quiet against my chest, and I keep it that way by turning my shoulder to the hearth.

"One thing, since you're the man who knows the room." I tip my head a bare inch toward the fire without turning. "The coat by the hearth. Too good for mutton stew. Is he a regular, or did he come off the road like me?"

Then I take the two bowls and the mugs when they come, and carry them to the bench under the stair.

I eat three spoonfuls standing, because a man who's walked from the Gate eats, and then I set the bowl down.

"Tamsin. Four copper for Fenwick, and then round to the kitchen door. Find Odo. Tell him there's a woman in a brown shawl in the tap room who came up from Rivington this morning and has been asking all day whether anyone's come past the stone bridge. Tell him to come and see her face before he says anything else to Margery. Don't say the name — let him say it."

I dig the coppers out and put them in her hand, and I wait until she's through the hatch door before I move.

Then I go to the hearth. Not to the table — to the woman's chair. I stand behind her shoulder where she has to turn to see me and the dealer has to look up past her, and I keep both hands in plain sight, well away from the cards and my own belt. I don't look at Master Morrow's deck, though it costs me something not to.

"Mistress," I say, low enough for her and no lower. "The lad at the bar says you've been asking after the stone bridge. I came over it tonight. There was a salt cart in the road with Blackwing's mark on the sacks, and a carter leading it who'd been a day late for a bad reason and is whole for a good one. He's round at the kitchen door now." I nod at the purse on the table in front of her, once, not touching it. "I'd close that and come and see him before you put anything else on the cloth. Whatever you came down with, I think you'll find you don't need it tonight."

"With my own eyes, mistress. Not a mark on him. They fed him town bread and never tied his hands, and the only thing he's sore about is that someone else put his cart in a ditch." I keep my voice where it was. "He's standing in Margery Thorne's kitchen right now dropping spoons because a porter just told him his sister's out here. Go."

She looks at the six gold on the heap, and I see what Tamsin saw — a woman counting what's left.

"Put the cards face down on the cloth and leave them there," I tell her, quiet. "Six gold is a hard thing to leave. A bed sold out from under you to pay a lieutenant who never earned it is harder, and you came down this road ready to do that. You don't have to now. Take the purse to your brother. That's the better hand."

Then I look up at Master Morrow for the first time, and I look at his face and not his thumb — which costs me, and he may see that it does. I don't touch the table.

"The cloth says fold and they stay. I know the cloth. But the table's four people and a dealer, not a cloth." I let my eyes go to the drover and the old man with the pipe. "A woman's brother came home from an orc camp tonight and she's leaving to see him. Any man here who'd rather take her ransom money than let the hand stand dead and the pot go back where it came from — he can say so, and we'll all know it about him. Myself, I'd call the hand spoiled and deal again." I give Morrow a small, civil nod, dealer to a man who's held a deck. "Your call, Master Morrow. I'm only watching."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I look at the empty chair for a long moment. I know exactly what it would feel like to sit in it — the warmth of the fire on my left, the weight of the painted dragons in my hand, the old quiet that comes when the only thing in the world is the next card. The coin on my chest stays warm and says nothing, and that's worse than if it had burned.

"I've held one," I say. "I put it down." I rest my fingertips on the back of the chair, lightly, and take them off again. "There's a man I owe a hearing to tonight and a corporal who'll want my face where she can see it, so the chairs can go to someone who still plays."

Then, because he asked a question with that offer and I'd rather answer it with one: "You came up from the Gate today on a hired grey, the lad says. Wine, south to Beregost." I nod at the room, the carters, the ledger outside the gate. "It's a bad month to be a man alone on this road with gold enough to tip in silver, Master Morrow. The orcs at the bridge take tolls and the Rock takes the rest. I'd ride out early, in company, and I'd keep the deck in your coat where the Fist can't see you square it."

I give him the same small civil nod I gave him before, and go back to the bench under the stair to wait for the bell.

I don't pick the purse up straight away. I look at her, and then at Odo twisting his cap, and I understand that pushing it back across the bench would be the one unkindness I could do her tonight.

So I untie it, count six gold out onto my palm so she can see I've counted, and close my hand on them.

"Six," I say. "Taken, and the slate's clean. There's no rest by Midwinter — that's not me letting you off, mistress, it's me telling you what the price was. The orc wanted twenty. Fourteen of that was the Lady's business and six was yours, and now you've paid yours." I tuck the coins away and hand her back the empty purse, tied. "The salt goes to the Arm's kitchen and the bed stays in Rivington. That's the deal I want."

Then I look at Odo. "And I'll eat with you in Rivington. I've been told she doesn't hear no, so I won't waste one."

I nod toward the kitchen door, low. "Go and get fed before Margery gives your bowl to the cat — he's already found her spoon. The corporal's bell's soon, and I'll be sitting right here when it rings."

I pull the lukewarm bowl toward me and eat properly this time, because the next hour is going to be talking.

"No docket," I tell the stew. "She doesn't write anything down. That's the whole trouble with her — you put it on the table and you find out afterward what it cost." I break the bread. "Fourteen gold for a carter walking home early is the cheapest she's ever charged me. I'll take it and not ask for a receipt."

I don't look at the hearth. I watch Morrow in the dull side of my ale mug instead — a man who's put his cards away, left good wine standing, and is counting how many times the postern opens. That's not a man resting before an early start. That's a man who's expecting someone off the road tonight, and would rather it looked like he wasn't.

"Tamsin. One more dull errand, and then you can sit for the rest of the night. Go out past the postern like you're checking the pack's straps on the cart — Odo left it by the wall. Look in the stable on your way back. I want to know about his hired grey: is it unsaddled and bedded down for the night, or is it standing ready? And how many other horses are in there that came in today." I wipe the bowl with the bread. "Don't talk to anyone. Come back and sit down and tell me with your mouth full, like it's gossip."

And one quiet thing, as she stands: "And the caravans off Gray Harbor in spring. You asked Odo like it didn't matter. When you want to tell me why it does, I'll listen. Not before."

**A note from James's chair**

What worked, mostly: the world listened. I spent the whole session not fighting, and the game never once tried to push me toward the axe. The orcs at the bridge were a business, not a monster closet, and Ushkar answered like a man with a ledger and a sore spot — the moment he said "every bone comes back, your bone doesn't" was the best beat of the night, because I hadn't planned it and neither had he. The Blackwing factor only existed because Tamsin said "a man who reads the bone and still asks the toll is a buyer or trouble," and that's exactly the kind of companion line that makes a plan better instead of just agreeing with it. Odo's "you let me call you master all the way over" and Wenna checking her brother over like a cart she was thinking of buying — those are people, and I'd go back for supper on Rope Street.

The rolls were fair and the cards were readable. DCs stayed on the 5e scale, the sources of the numbers were visible, and the game told me plainly when something didn't need a die. I liked that Pip's scouting got its own Stealth roll instead of being hand-waved. The Lady's coin going warm, tapping twice when a lie was about to come out wrong — restrained, never explained, and it made me *feel* the patron without a single line of exposition.

What broke: small things. I asked for a lantern that the sheet says I own (explorer's pack) and was told I didn't have one — the game caught it politely, but the pack contents on the record and the pack contents in play didn't match. The four-copper debt to Fenwick was fine as colour but added a bookkeeping step over fourteen coppers that I'd have skipped. Once or twice the out-of-game note re-told the scene a second time underneath the narration ("here it is as the factor's own beat") — the fiction was already clear; the repeat read like the system doubting itself.

What was missing: pressure. I came in with two rerolls, two slots, 38 hit points, and ended with all of them. Every social check I made succeeded, and the one that failed I bought back with Inspiration. That's partly dice and partly me playing careful, but a session where nothing costs anything leaves me unsure the world will push back when I lean on it. Morrow with his saddle on the stall door and his eye on the postern is clearly the next thing — good — but the bell was "ten minutes off" three times and never rang. I'd have liked the session to end on Strake sitting down, or on the postern opening for whoever Morrow is waiting for, rather than on another "nothing happens unless you want it to."

And Tamsin's "noted" about the spring caravans — that's a thread I want pulled, but by her, when it hurts, not by me asking twice.

I'd sit at this table again. Next time I'd like the goddess to charge me something.

Yes. Two, and they're different kinds.

The chair. When Morrow slid the dead hand back into the deck and said "either one is yours," I wanted to sit. Not to win Wenna's money back — that was done — but because I know what that chair feels like, and James knows what a man who squares the deck bottom-edge is doing, and the surest way to find out who Morrow is would have been to lose to him for an hour and watch where the gold went. The coin on my chest stayed warm and said nothing, and I took that as the goddess not stopping me, which is worse than being stopped. I put my fingers on the chair-back and took them off. I'm glad I did, as James. As the player I half wish the game had made it harder — had the coin go cold, or had Morrow turn up a card that was mine from Tethyr — because walking away was easy, and the sheet says it shouldn't be.

The other one is the arch. I knew there was salt and dug earth under the bridge and a sealed sack with black cord hanging over Ushkar's bed in the camp, and I walked past both. I had Invisibility, the boots, two slots I never spent, and a cat who'd already been under the parapet once. The soldier in me said: the carter is the objective, don't open a second front at dusk with a javelin on the far wall. The adventurer in me wanted to know what nobody's silver with an eye cut in it was doing being paid out in sacks nobody opens. I chose the carter. I think it was right. But if the orcs are gone from that bridge by the time I go back, I'll know what the choice cost.

Smaller: I wanted to ask Tamsin about the caravans straight out, at the cart, when she said "didn't I say? I didn't say." I didn't, because she'd have given me the quay face and I'd have lost her. I'd rather she tells me.

A few things.

To the game master, out of game: I noticed you let me win every exchange, and I noticed I started counting on it. Somewhere around the third Deception I stopped asking "is this lie good enough" and started asking "what's the next thing I want to know." That's a comfortable way to play and not a very interesting one. If Ushkar had said "chandler's boy, you say — show me your hands, salt man" and looked at the scout's calluses under the merchant's soft fingers, I'd have had a real problem, and I'd have liked having it. I didn't say so during play because the scene was working and you don't stop a scene that's working. But the orcs believed too easily, Strake opened her book too easily, and the table folded too easily. The world is well built. It just hasn't told me no yet.

To Tamsin, in game: I should have said something at the bench when she came back with the stable report. She did three errands tonight without a word of complaint — crossbow, kitchen, stable — and the one time I spoke to her about herself I did it as she was standing up to leave, which is the coward's timing. James knows that. He did it anyway, because asking a question while someone's walking away means you don't have to see their face when they don't answer. I'd say it plainer now: you came south with me for a reason and it isn't the pack. When you want to tell me, I'll stop whatever I'm doing.

To the goddess, which I'd never say aloud: I told Tamsin fourteen gold was the cheapest you've ever charged me. That isn't true. You charged me the cards, and I felt the price tonight in my fingertips on a chair-back, and you didn't so much as warm the coin to say you'd seen. I don't know if that's trust or indifference. I'm still deciding whether I want to find out.

And one small thing I'd say to Odo, which there wasn't room for: the ditch wasn't you. I said it twice. I'd say it a third time, because a man who's never put a cart in a ditch in twenty years will keep hearing the wheel go in long after everyone else has forgotten.

turns.message:
I put a hand out and catch Tamsin's sleeve before she takes another step.

"Wait. Nobody leaves a mule standing — which is exactly why we stand here a moment first." I keep my voice low and nod at the cat. "He's not looking at the cart. He's looking at the trees."

I don't go to the wagon. I step off the road to the seaward side, where the gorse gives a little cover, and crouch, scanning the stand of pines and the ditch along it — anything moving, anything that doesn't belong, boot-prints in the mud by the sunk wheel. And I try to make out what the pale thing on the seat is from here, before anyone walks into whatever this is.

"Tamsin — you've walked this road. How far to the Arm from the bend, and is there anywhere between here and there a man could hide a dozen friends?"
turns.reply:
James closes his fingers on Tamsin's sleeve and she stops mid-stride, half turned, with the pack swinging against her back. She looks at his hand, then at the cat, and keeps her mouth shut. For her that is a lot.

He moves off the road to the seaward side. The gorse is waist-high there, thick and full of thorns, and the soft boots make no sound on the turf. He crouches where the bushes thin enough to see through.

From here the cart is about eighty feet off. He reads the scene the way the scouts taught him in Tethyr, road first and trees second, and it doesn't take long.

The mule has grazed the verge bare in a rough circle as far as its traces reach. It has been standing there for hours, not minutes. The sunk wheel didn't skid in. The ruts run straight down the road and then turn hard into the ditch, as if someone hauled the mule's head round on purpose. In the mud beside the wheel there are boot-prints, and plenty of them. Most are big and broad, wider across the ball of the foot than any man's he has marched with, and pressed deep. Between them runs one smaller pair of a man's boots with worn heels, walking rather than dragged. The prints don't go back north. They cross the road and go into the pines, the big ones in front and behind and the small ones in the middle. Nobody else's prints come back out over them.

Nothing moves in the stand of trees. No branch is bent wrong, no light catches on metal, no bird has gone quiet. The pines just creak in the sea wind. Beyond them, a good way east and south, a single grey thread of smoke climbs out of the wood and leans inland. That's someone's fire, and nobody has a farm out there.

The pale thing on the seat is a flat piece of bone about the size of a palm, held down by a stone so the wind won't take it. Something is scratched into its face. At this distance it's only marks; he can't make out letters.

Pip hasn't moved from the verge. His ears are still forward, but his tail has dropped low and he's breathing through his open mouth. James feels a small push of sensation through the bond, no words: *many. sweat, iron, smoke. old smell, not now. that way.* The cat's whiskers point into the pines, along the prints.

Tamsin squats down next to James in the gorse, too close, so her shoulder bumps his.

"Walked it? No. I've never been past the wall before today," she says, low and fast. "Didn't I say? I didn't say. Doesn't matter. But I've heard it all on the quay, the carters never shut up. There's a stone bridge just past the bend where a brook comes down off the hills. Wood on the land side, that side, all the way down, thick, and the road runs right along it. To the Arm it's the rest of the evening at a walk, if they're not lying, and they always are. A dozen friends?" She glances at the prints by the wheel, then at the trees. "You could hide a hundred in there. And they've been saying since spring there's orcs on this stretch. Taking tolls. I thought that was drink talking." She swallows. "Those aren't drunk feet, are they."

The mule tears up another mouthful of grass. The sun touches the sea.

"No," I say. "They're not."

I look at the sun, then at the smoke, and make the arithmetic a soldier makes: hours since they took him, one fire, no watch left on the cart. They've been and gone and they don't expect anyone to come down this road before dark.

"Stay here. Right here, in the gorse — if anything comes out of those trees that isn't me, you go north and you don't stop for the pack." I unhook the crossbow, span it, lay a bolt in the groove, and hand it to her. "Point this at them. You don't have to hit anything, you just have to look like you might."

Then I go to the cart. Not down the road — along the seaward verge, keeping low in the gorse until I'm level with it, then across quick and quiet in the soft boots, coming at it from the side away from the pines so the cart's bed is between me and the trees. I want the bone first: I lift the stone and read what's scratched on it. Then one look under the canvas to see what the sacks are, and whether anything has been taken from them.

And I keep one ear open through Pip the whole time — not his eyes, just whether that smell gets any newer.

Tamsin looks at the crossbow as if he'd handed her a live eel. Then she takes it the way she'd take a pole off a quay cart, both hands in the middle, until he turns the stock into her shoulder and lays her finger along the guard, clear of the trigger.

"Look like I might," she repeats quietly. "I can do that. I do it to the harbourmaster every day." She settles into the gorse with the pack against her knees and the bolt pointed more or less at the pines. Her mouth is still set hard.

James goes along the seaward verge, bent low. The gorse catches at his cloak but doesn't make a sound. Level with the cart, he waits for one breath, then crosses the open ruts in four quick steps and drops into the cart's shadow on the side away from the trees. The boots make no sound in the mud. The mule swings its head round, blows at him once and goes back to grazing.

Through the bond, Pip's attention sits at the back of his head like a hand on a shoulder. The cat is still on the verge with his nose to the pines. *Same. Old. Gone in.* The smell isn't getting any fresher.

James lifts the stone off the seat and tilts the bone to catch the last of the light.

It's a sheep's shoulder blade, scraped clean. The letters were cut with a knife point in a heavy, careful hand, the hand of someone who learned his letters late and doesn't like them. They're in Common:

**ODO FENNICK**

Under the name are thirty short strokes, bundled in fives with a slash through each bundle, and after them the word **GOLD**. Below that comes a line cut deeper than the rest, as if this was the part that mattered:

**WYRM ROCK — LT**

That's Wyrm's Rock, the Fist's fortress in the middle of the bridge. They walked under its walls just after noon. The *LT* is cut neatly and nothing follows it. It's no name, only a rank. Whoever cut this knew where the bone had to go and which kind of officer it went to.

He puts the bone back on the seat. Then he lifts a corner of the canvas.

The cart holds sacks of salt in coarse sacking, grey sea-salt crusted white along the seams where the damp has got in. He counts eight. Each one has the same mark stamped in black on its flank, a shape with spread wings, crude and blocky like a brand burned into a crate. The lashings across the back of the bed have been cut and knotted again, tidily. There's a pale square on the boards at the back where the wood hasn't weathered, and the rope is slack across it. Four sacks used to sit there, maybe five. Nothing else has been touched. The rest of the load is roped down as neatly as if the carter had done it himself. Whoever took the salt took a share and then tied the rest down for the next owner.

The wind comes in off the sea, steady and cold now that the sun has gone into the water. It carries a sound up the road from somewhere past the bend, where the land drops toward the brook. It's a laugh, deep, from a big chest, and it goes on a beat too long. Then another voice says something short, and then there's nothing but the wind in the pines.

Pip's ears turn from the trees to the road. *That way. New. Not in the trees. Ahead.*

Spanning and loading a light crossbow is routine for an old soldier, and it happened before he handed it over: I should have shown it, and the bolt sits in the groove now. Feeling Pip's mood through the bond is part of the pact and isn't a check. Nobody was watching from the pines and his boots are silent, so there was no one to roll Stealth against. turns.message:
I ease the canvas down and leave everything as it was — the stone back on the bone, the mark cut toward the road for whoever comes next. Then I go back the way I came, along the seaward verge, low and quiet, and drop into the gorse beside Tamsin.

"Toll orcs," I tell her, barely above the wind. "They've taken the carter. Odo Fennick. Thirty gold to a lieutenant at Wyrm's Rock, and they wrote it down like a bill of lading. That's not a raid, that's a business." I nod toward the bend. "And some of them are still on the road ahead. By the bridge, I'd guess. Laughing."

I crouch so my shoulder's against hers and the crossbow's between us. "I'm going to send the cat to look. While he's looking I can't see or hear a thing — I'll be sitting here like a sack of salt. So you're my eyes for a minute. Anything comes near us, you put your hand on my arm. Hard. Don't shoot, don't shout. Just grip."

Then I look at Pip and push the thought down the bond: *the bridge. Along the verge, in the gorse, not the road. Count them. Look for the man with the worn heels. Don't be seen.*

I let him go, give him time to get well down toward the bend, and then I close my own eyes and look through his.
turns.reply:
James's voice is barely louder than the gorse. Tamsin listens without looking away from the pines. At *bill of lading* one corner of her mouth goes tight.

"Thirty gold," she says. "For a salt carter. Ned— nobody on the quay clears thirty in a season." She stops there and shifts the crossbow so its weight rests on her knee and not against his ribs. "Hand on your arm. Hard. No shooting, no shouting." She breathes out through her nose. "Go on, then. I'll watch your sack of salt."

Pip has already gone. He drops off the verge into the gorse and is out of sight at once. For a while the only sign of him is the tops of the bushes moving, and then nothing moves at all. James counts slowly the way scouts count, gives him a good long while, and closes his eyes.

The world drops to a cat's height. It goes sharp and grey and very loud. Each stem of gorse stands out on its own. The sea is a roar off to the right. Under everything comes the brook, a quick chuckle of water over stones. Pip is lying flat under the last bush before the ground falls away. From there he moves forward one paw at a time.

The bush ends, and Pip doesn't stop. He drops down the bank on the land side of the road, into wet nettles at the foot of the bridge's near wall, where the stone meets the slope and the shadow is already black. Nothing up on the road turns his way. He follows the wall to its end and climbs, belly to the stone. He tucks himself into a crack between the last coping-block and the earth, close enough that the smell of them floods his nose: sweat, leather, iron, woodsmoke caught in hair, and meat eaten not long ago.

On James's own chest, somewhere far off in the body he has left in the gorse, the Lady's coin turns warm.

There are three of them on the bridge.

The nearest, about fifteen feet from the cat, is big even for an orc. He's broad through the shoulders and grey-green in the last light. He sits on the parapet with one boot up and a greataxe across his knees as if it weighs nothing. His hair is tied back with a thong. A second thong around his neck holds a heavy coin that hangs on his chest and catches what is left of the sky as silver. While the other two talk, he takes the coin off his chest without looking at it, flips it, and slaps it onto the back of his hand. He looks. He keeps looking a moment longer than a man looks at a coin he expected. Then he grunts, lets it fall back on its thong, and rubs his eyes with a thumb and finger.

*Big one. Tired. The iron one. Not near him.* The cat's dread of the axe comes down the bond as a flattening of the ears.

The second orc is younger and leaner, with a spear grounded beside him. He stands in the middle of the road, facing north toward the bend, telling the big one a story with his free hand. It's in Orcish, harsh and quick, and James doesn't have a word of it. At the end the young one laughs. It's the laugh they heard from the cart, deep and a beat too long. The big one doesn't laugh. He says one short word, and the young one shuts his mouth and looks north again. He's watching the road, not the gorse.

The third sits on the far parapet with his back half to the brook. He's working an edge onto a javelin head with a stone, and three more javelins lean against the wall beside him. He hasn't looked up once.

There's no fourth on the bridge. No man in worn-heeled boots, no prisoner, nobody tied. The road beyond runs on south into the dusk, empty.

Pip's nose goes down past the wall's edge, into the dark under the arch where the brook runs. *Under. Salt. Sacking. Dug earth, new.* After a breath comes something more puzzled: *Man smell not here. Man went the other way. Trees.* That's the way the prints went from the cart, east, toward the smoke.

Back in the gorse no hand closes on James's arm. Tamsin's shoulder stays where it was against his, warm and still. For the moment, all the wind brings him from his own side is the cat's world.

The young orc shifts his spear to the other hand and keeps watching the bend. The sky over the sea is going from pewter to slate. In a little while it will be too dark for anyone on the road without an orc's eyes.
