They've buried the salt under the arch and the man went east, into the wood, toward that fire."

I rub my thumb over the coin on my chest. It's still warm.

"The big one flips a coin. Keeps looking at it like it's giving him an answer he doesn't like." I'm quiet a moment. "Tamsin, I want you to hear this plain, because I know what you'd do and I'd rather you didn't. Three orcs is a fight I can win from eighty feet if the dice fall right, and a fight that kills us both if they don't — the one with the javelins would have you before you'd finished looking brave. So I'm not going to start one. Not in the dark, not with the carter out of reach.

"Here's what I'm turning over. They're not raiders, they're tollmen. Tollmen talk. A traveller walks up to the bridge in the last light with a porter and a mule he found standing in the road, and asks what the toll is. That traveller doesn't have to be me — I can wear another man's face. What I want out of it isn't the bridge. It's where Odo Fennick is and what they'll take for him, from the mouth of the one who flips the coin." I look at her. "And you'd be standing behind me the whole time with that crossbow and your harbourmaster face. Can you do that and not do anything else?"

The weight of the cat's senses lifts off him and he's back in his own body: cold face, gorse thorns at his knee, Tamsin's shoulder warm against his. The sea is louder from here. Down the bond he feels Pip take the order. The cat doesn't answer in words, just a flick of his attention as he turns around in the crack and starts down the wall.

Pip comes back the way he went: down into the nettles, along the foot of the wall, up the bank. Nobody on the bridge turns his way. The young orc keeps watching the bend and the whetstone keeps scraping. A while later the gorse beside James shivers and the cat pushes in under his elbow. His coat is wet from the nettles and he smells of the brook. He sits down and starts washing a paw as if he'd only been out to the end of the garden.

Tamsin hears the count without interrupting. When he gets to *buried the salt under the arch* her eyebrows go up. When he says *the man went east* she looks at the smoke, and she keeps looking at it while he gets to the part about her.

She doesn't answer right away. She shifts the crossbow on her knee, finger still along the guard where he put it.

"Stand behind you. Hold this. Do nothing else," she says, low, like a list being checked off. Then, in her ordinary quick voice: "Yes. I can. I've stood behind the harbourmaster while he told a Calishite captain his berth fee had doubled, and I kept my face. This is the same, only bigger and greener."

She chews her lip.

"But listen, about the mule. You walk up there with their mule and their cart, that's not *a traveller*. That's someone who's been to the cart and read the bone. They left that bone for somebody to carry north. Fine, maybe that's who you want to be. But a man who stopped to read a ransom and still walks up and asks the toll? On the quay, a man who walks up already knowing the price is either a buyer or trouble, and they'll look at you the way you'd look at either." She lifts one shoulder. "So which is he? The one in the other face. Is he buying the carter back, or does he just want to know the price?"

The sky over the water has gone from slate to ink at the bottom edge. On the bridge, where they can't see it, the whetstone has stopped.

"Buyer," I say. "You're right, and it's a good catch. A traveller is wrong. A man who reads the bone and walks on is either a fool or the Fist, and I don't want to be either tonight."

I get my feet under me. "There was a mark on the sacks. Wings, black, stamped like a brand. That's somebody's salt house. So the man who walks up to the bridge is the salt house's factor — the fellow who signs for the carter's wages. Odo didn't come back, the factor rode south to find out why, found his cart in the ditch with a bill on the seat, and now he wants his mule, his man and the balance of his salt, and he's irritated about the price. That man is allowed to know the carter's name. He's allowed to be short with them. He's *expected* to haggle." I glance at her. "And a factor doesn't walk alone. He brings a hand off the quay who looks like she'd enjoy it if someone said no."

I take the Lady's coin between finger and thumb a moment. Still warm. The big orc flipping his own silver — I file that away.

Then I let the mask go on. Mask of Many Faces: a softer, older face than mine, forty-odd, clean-shaven, with the jowls of a man who eats at other people's expense; the cloak becomes a good brown merchant's coat with a bit of fur at the collar; the rod in my hand reads as a walking stick with a brass knob. I keep my own boots.

"Pip — stay in the gorse. Watch the javelin-man. If he stands up with one in his hand, I want to feel it."

I go back along the verge to the cart, take the mule's headstall, and talk to it until it decides I'm a person worth following. Then the three of us go round the bend onto the open road and toward the bridge at a walk, the cart creaking behind, Tamsin a pace back on my left with the crossbow carried low and loaded. Forty feet out, where the young one can see me plain, I stop, plant the stick, and call out in the voice of a man who has been inconvenienced all day:

"Evening. I'm looking for whoever wrote me a bill for thirty gold. I'll talk to him and no one else — and I'll have my mule back first, since nobody charged me for the loan of it."

Tamsin hears him out with her head on one side. At *factor* she nods once, the way she'd nod at a fair price on the quay.

"Blackwing," she says. "The wings. It's Blackwing Salts, the chandlery off Gray Harbor. Half the inns on the Way buy from them. If you're their man, you're sour, you're tight with money, and you think orcs are a line in the ledger." One corner of her mouth twitches. "I've carried for their factors. I know the face."

Then his face stops being his. The mask settles over him the way a coat does. He's heavier in the jaw and softer under the chin, and his hair has gone grey at the temples. The grey infantry cloak hangs as good brown wool with a strip of fur at the collar, and the rod is a walking stick with a brass knob. Tamsin looks him up and down and breathes out through her nose.

"Oh, that's horrible," she whispers. "That's exactly him."

Pip goes off into the gorse toward the bend without a sound, low and fast, and his attention settles at the back of James's head again.

The mule doesn't object to being led. It does object to the ditch. When James takes the headstall and asks it to walk on, it leans into the collar and the sunk wheel doesn't move. Tamsin lays the crossbow in the grass with the bolt still in it, gets her shoulder under the tailboard and says "*Hup*" the way she must say it a hundred times a day on the quay. Mule and porter heave together and the wheel comes out of the mud with a sucking lurch. She picks the crossbow up again, wipes her hands on her trousers and falls in a pace behind him on his left.

They go round the bend. The road drops toward the brook, and the bridge is there: low grey stone, the water loud under it, and three dark shapes against a sky that has almost no colour left. The young one sees them first. Of course he does. He has been watching this bend for hours, and in this light his eyes are better than theirs.

He shouts something in Orcish and brings the spear up level.

Down the bond, sharp and sudden: *Up. The thrower is up. One in his hand.* Through the cat's eyes, low among the nettles at the bridge end, James sees the javelin orc on his feet on the far parapet. His arm is cocked and ready but he hasn't thrown.

The big one doesn't stand at first. He turns his head, looks at the cart, at the mule and at the fat man in the fur collar, and only then gets off the parapet. The greataxe comes with him in one hand, head down, the way a man carries a tool.

Forty feet out, James plants the stick and calls across the water noise in the voice of a man who has been put out all day.

Ushkar listens all the way to the end. He looks at the fur collar, the fat hands, the brass-knobbed stick, and the quay girl behind with the crossbow and the sour face. For a moment he looks at James the way James has watched men look at a dealer they've decided is honest. Then he stops thinking about whether the factor is real and starts thinking about the factor's money.

He says one word in Orcish without turning his head. The young one's spearpoint drops to the road. On the far parapet the javelin goes down to rest against the stone. *Down,* Pip reports. *Still holding it.*

Then the big orc does something James didn't expect. He walks off the bridge toward them alone and leaves the other two behind. He stops ten feet off, close enough that the brook covers his voice from his own men, and rests the axe head on the road.

This close, James's own eyes can do what the cat's did. The silver on the thong is the size of a big man's thumbnail and too heavy to be any coin of the Gate. On the face turned outward, worn soft by handling, is a woman's profile smiling at nothing. Under the merchant's coat, the Lady's coin on James's chest goes from warm to hot for the space of a breath, like a hand laid flat on his breastbone, and then it's only warm again.

"Salt man," the orc says. His Common is low and heavy. Every word sounds like something he has paid for. "Bill is not for you. Bill goes to the Rock. They pay." He tips his chin at the mule. "Mule, take. Is why we leave it. Cart goes north, bone goes with it." He looks past James at Tamsin and her crossbow for exactly as long as it takes to dismiss them both, then back again. "Your man is in the trees. Dry. Fed. Nobody hit him."

He waits. Behind him, the young one has started edging closer to hear, and the big one doesn't look round. He only lowers his voice further.

"You carry gold, salt man? Here?" One heavy finger taps the silver on his chest, and he doesn't flip it. "Thirty. In my hand, not to the Rock. Then he walks out of trees tonight, not in three days."

The voice, the face, the impatience and the bill he wants settled all hang together without a seam, and the big orc takes James for exactly who he claims to be: Blackwing Salts' factor, come south in person to buy back his carter. From here on he's bargaining with a salt man, not sizing up a stranger. For a moment, somewhere at the back of James's head, there's the feeling of a card turned face up that he never had to play.

Then he sets the flat of it across his knee and leans on it. It breaks with a dry crack. He breaks the halves again, steps to the edge of the road and drops the pieces over the bank. The brook takes them without a sound anyone can hear over the water.

He listens to the part about the rider without moving. At *horse's shoes* his eyes narrow slightly. At *somebody is paying to be nobody* his thumb goes to the thong at his neck, rests on the silver and stays there. He doesn't flip it.

"Hands," he says at last. "Shoes. I look." He's quiet for a moment, and then he taps two thick fingers once against his own chest, below the coin, where the kerchief went. "Ushkar. Word comes, it comes from Ushkar. Not from bone."

Then the factor turns his back on the axe and walks to the cart, slow and heavy-footed on his sore merchant's feet.

Nothing comes after him. At the back of his head Pip keeps up his small reports: *Thrower sits. Big one stands. Watching you go.* Then, after a moment: *Big one turns. Goes to the bridge.* Under the brown coat the Lady's coin lies warm and quiet on his breastbone.

Odo is still at the mule's head with one hand flat on its neck. He looks up as the factor comes near and keeps his voice low, the way a man does with orcs thirty feet off.

"Master." He swallows. His voice is still rough. "She's pointed south. Arm's kitchen's waiting on this salt, they're paid half already, the rest on the barrels." He glances at the eight sacks under the canvas, then back at the factor's face. "We turning her round for the Gate? Or do I take what's left on down?"

turns.message:
"Down," I say, loud enough to carry. "I didn't ride all this way to carry salt back to the sea. The Arm's paid half; the Arm gets its barrels. Walk her on, and keep her to the middle of the bridge."

Then quieter, for Odo alone, as I fall in beside the mule's head: "And keep your mouth shut till the water's behind us. All of it. I'll explain the rest when we can't be heard."

I push down the bond: *Pip. Stay low. Come once we're over.*

We cross as a factor crosses — the carter leading, the cart creaking, Tamsin a pace behind me with the crossbow carried low, me in the middle with the stick, not hurrying and not looking at the thrower. As we pass Ushkar on the parapet I give him the one civil nod a merchant gives a man he's just settled with, and nothing more.

Once the bridge is a dark shape behind us and the brook is only a sound, I let my shoulders come down a little, and ask Odo, low, without breaking stride: "Now. The camp. How many were there, really? Who gave the orders — the big one, or somebody else? And did anyone come to that fire today who wasn't an orc?"
turns.reply:
The factor's voice carries over the water. "Walk her on." Odo takes the headstall without a word and clicks his tongue, and the mule leans into the collar. The cart creaks forward.

When the factor drops his voice for Odo alone, the carter's eyes flick to him once and go back to the road. He nods and says nothing. He's done what paymasters tell him his whole life.

*Low,* comes back down the bond, and Pip flattens deeper into the nettles.

They cross at a walk. The wheels rumble hollow on the stone, and under them the brook runs loud and black over whatever is buried there. The javelin orc sits on the far parapet with the shaft across his knees, and his head turns slowly to follow them. Tamsin keeps a pace behind on the left with the crossbow low and her quay face on.

Ushkar sits on the near parapet again with one boot up and the axe across his knees. As the factor passes he gives him the civil nod a merchant gives a man he has finished doing business with. The big orc watches him do it. After a moment he dips his chin once, very slightly, and looks back up the road toward the bend as if they'd already gone.

Then the stone is behind them and the road is earth again, climbing gently south through the dark. The brook fades to a murmur and then to nothing. Somewhere back there a small weight drops off a bank, and a little later Pip trots past the wheel, damp and smelling of nettles. He falls in beside the mule as if he had always walked there. The mule doesn't object.

The factor's shoulders come down a finger's width. He asks his questions low, without breaking stride.

Odo keeps his eyes on the ruts for a while. When he answers, the words come in a rush, the way they do from a man who has had nobody to talk to all day.

"Two, at the fire. The scarred one and the one with the rope. Then the young one come running and said something and they all got up." He swallows. "The big one never come to the camp. Not while I was there. But they said his name. Ushkar. Every time the young one wanted something, the scarred one'd say *Ushkar* and that was the end of it." He shakes his head. "Orders was his. Even with him on the bridge."

The mule's ears twitch. Odo puts a hand on its neck without looking.

"Nobody else come. No man. Just them and me and the fire." He frowns at the road. "They gave me bread, master. Town bread, a proper loaf. They never tied me. The scarred one sat across the fire all day like a dog at a door, and when I had to piss he walked me to a tree and turned his back." He sounds more bothered by that than by anything else. "What kind of orcs turn their back?"

He goes quiet for a few steps. Then the rest comes out.

"There was a sack. Hung off a branch over where the big one sleeps, I reckon, a hide laid out under it. Little cloth sack, heavy, the way coin hangs. Black cord round the neck and a blob of black wax on the knot. Not broke." He glances up at the factor's soft jowls and away again. "The young one kept looking at it. The scarred one kept looking at the young one."

Then, because it has been sitting in him since the ditch: "And the ditch weren't me. I saw them on the bridge and tried to turn her round, and they come out of the gorse and hauled her head over. I never put her in on my own. Twenty years, I never put a cart in a ditch."

Behind them Tamsin lets out a long breath through her nose. She doesn't speak, but James can feel her listening to every word.

Odo walks a few more paces, then says the thing a carter can't leave alone.

"The four sacks they had off the back, master. Is that on me?"

*(Out of game: the factor's face has roughly a quarter of an hour left before it falls away, and Odo is walking right beside you.)*

turns.message:
"No," I say. "The four sacks aren't on you. Nor's the ditch. Twenty years says you don't put a cart in a ditch, and I believe twenty years."

I walk a few more paces, then stop the mule with a hand on the headstall, so the three of us stand together in the dark with the cart between us and the wind.

"Odo. Listen, because you've got maybe a quarter-hour to get used to this before you see it with your own eyes." I keep my voice level and low. "There is no Master Hallam, and there's no gout, and Blackwing Salts didn't send anyone. I'm not your factor. I'm a traveller who found your cart standing in the road with a bill on the seat, and I didn't like the arithmetic, so I borrowed a face that could pay it. This girl's a porter off the quay who's carried your house's salt and knew what your factors look like. That's all we are."

I let the mask go. The brown coat is a grey soldier's cloak again, the stick is a dark rod with a silver coin set in it, and the soft jowls are a leaner, younger face with a scout's eyes. I let him look.

"James Worgen. The twenty gold was mine, and I'm not asking you or Blackwing for it back. What I am asking is this. When you get to the Arm, you'll tell the story — you'd be no carter if you didn't. Tell it true. But tell it the way it was: the orcs fed you and never tied you and took thirty-odd gold for a bill to Wyrm's Rock. Don't make the big one a monster he wasn't and don't make me a hero I wasn't. Somewhere between that bridge and that fortress there's a lieutenant eating carters' wages, and I'd like the story to reach him in a shape that makes him nervous."

I nod at the mule. "Now walk her on. The Arm's kitchen wants its salt, and I want a chair by a fire where nobody's holding a javelin."
turns.reply:
Odo walks the next few paces with his eyes on the ruts. When the factor says *I believe twenty years*, his jaw works and he nods at the road. He doesn't say anything, but he walks a little straighter for it.

Then the mule stops under the hand on its headstall. The three of them stand together in the dark with the cart creaking to rest between them and the sea wind.

Odo listens to all of it with his head down, the way he's listened to paymasters his whole life. At *there is no Master Hallam* his shoulders go still. At *borrowed a face* he looks up.

The fur collar is gone. The brown wool turns back into a grey soldier's cloak with a regimental patch on the shoulder. The brass-knobbed stick is a short dark rod with a silver coin set in its head. The soft jowls are gone too. The face is leaner and ten years younger, with a scout's eyes, the face of a man who has slept outdoors more than in. There's not much light out here, only starlight and the pale road, but it's enough. Odo takes half a step back with his hand flat on the mule's neck and looks for a long moment.

"Knew it," he says. His voice is still hoarse. "Back on the bridge. Knew I didn't know you." He swallows. "Then you shouted at me, and I stopped knowing it."

A breath goes out of him that isn't quite a laugh.

"You let me call you master. All the way over."

He keeps looking at James's face. Then he looks at Tamsin, who gives him a small shrug that says *quay*, and back at James.

"Twenty gold." He says it as if he's weighing a sack. "That's near a season, for me. I heard you. You're not asking." He shakes his head once. "Don't matter what you ask. I owe it. That's mine to owe, not yours to let off."

The mule tugs at its bit, wanting to go on. Odo doesn't let it.

"Tell it true. Aye. I don't know how to tell it any other way." He frowns hard at the road ahead. "But I'll not make the big one kind, either. He fed me, and he never tied me, and he took me off my own cart in front of my own mule. I'll say all three."

He's quiet for a few breaths, and something else comes up in him.

"The Rock. That bone was going to the Rock." He looks north, though there's nothing to see but dark. "My sister's in Rivington, just over the water from it. Wenna. If the Fist had sent to her saying thirty gold..." He stops. "She'd have found it. Sold the bed out from under herself. She'll be fretting already. Cart's a day late and I'm never late."

Tamsin has been standing with the crossbow down at her side, quietly taking all of this in. "Well," she says, "you're not late now, are you? You're early. Nobody on the Way's ever come out of an orc camp early." She looks at James's own face and lets her own face go back to its ordinary shape for the first time in an hour. "I liked the other one better. He was sourer. You knew where you stood."

Odo almost smiles at that. He clicks his tongue, and the mule leans into the collar again. The cart rolls on south, and Pip falls in beside the wheel. The road climbs gently into the dark, and the Friendly Arm is still most of the evening's walk ahead.

The road ahead is quiet, and nothing is waiting between here and the Arm's gate unless you want something.

turns.message:
I let the cart roll on a dozen paces before I fall in beside Odo again, and this time I'm not a factor and not anyone's master — just a man walking beside a mule in the dark. I get the lantern out of my pack and hang it from the cart's tail-hook, lit low, so the Arm sees honest carters coming and not shadows.

"Wenna'll hear you're whole before she hears you were taken, if you walk fast enough. That's worth more than twenty gold, so call us square." I don't give him room to argue it.

Then, as we climb, I turn the Lady's coin over on its cord under my cloak, and think about the other one: a woman going south alone in spring, with no gold, who paid a toll with a piece of silver that lands how it likes and has an eye cut into its back. The coin on my chest went hot when it saw its sister. I don't say any of that aloud.

What I say is to Tamsin, low. "That rider. Bright new silver, not a scratch, never spent. You know the quay. Where does coin like that come from in the Gate — who handles money nobody's touched? The Counting House? A patriar's strongroom? Because whoever's paying thirty gold a carter to look like a lieutenant isn't paying it out of a soldier's wages."

And to Odo: "The Arm. Who's behind the bar there who hears everything and forgets nothing? When you tell your story tonight, I want to know whose ears it's falling on."
turns.reply:
Odo lets the cart roll on. When James falls in beside him at the mule's head, the carter glances sideways once, at the grey cloak and the lean face, as if checking that the fat man really has gone.

At *call us square* his jaw works. He walks a few paces with nothing to say for it.

"Square, you say," he says at last. "I heard you." He clicks his tongue at the mule. "Wenna'll want to feed you. Don't tell her no. She don't hear no."

That's all the agreement he gives. The road climbs on through the dark, and the cart creaks.

Tamsin has been walking with the crossbow in the crook of her arm like a broom handle. When James drops his voice for her she moves up on his other side.

"New silver?" She doesn't have to think about it. "Counting House. Has to be. Nobody else in the Gate hands out coin that's never been in a pocket. You take a letter of credit up there, a clerk goes into the back and comes out with a sack, bright as fish scales. I've carried them down to ships. Canvas bags with the House's stamp on, red cord, and a lead seal on the knot so you know nobody's had a hand in it."

Odo's head turns.

"Weren't red," he says. "That sack at the fire. Black cord. Black wax on the knot." He frowns at the road. "No stamp I saw. Mind, it were dark under that branch."

Tamsin opens her mouth, shuts it again, and looks at James.

"Well," she says, slower, "who draws coin from the House, then? Anyone with an account. Merchants. The patriar houses. Their stewards come down from the Upper City with a guard and a face like they're doing you a favour. And the Fist. Their paymaster's wagon goes down Wide past the quay every tenday with four Fist sitting on the chest." She shrugs. "That's half the city with money worth stealing. And it never stays new on the quay. By sundown it's in some tavern till and it smells of fish."

The mule blows and leans into the slope. Odo answers the other question without being asked twice, short, the way he'd give directions to a yard.

"Bar's a lad called Fenwick. Talks to everyone. Forgets it all by morning." He shakes his head. "Not him. Kitchen. Margery Thorne, the cook. She buys my salt. Everything said in that common room comes back through the hatch with the plates, and she don't forget a word of it. Don't tell you, neither, unless she likes you." He walks a few steps. "And there's Fist at the gate. A corporal. Strake, a woman. Writes every cart into a book, what it's carrying and who's driving. Wrote me in going north last month." He rubs his stubble. "She'll want to know why I'm a day late. She asks."

Behind them the road falls away into the dark toward the brook. Ahead it keeps climbing under the stars, empty, with the Arm still a long walk off.

*(Out of game: there's no lantern in your pack. Tamsin is carrying ten torches and a tinderbox, and you have the Light cantrip. Tell me which one you want on the tail-hook, if either, and I'll put it there.)*

turns.message:
"A torch, then. Honest fire for honest carters." I take one from Tamsin's pack, light it from her tinderbox, wedge it in the tail-hook and knock it down to a low glow — enough that the Arm's gate sees a cart with a lamp, not three shadows coming out of the orc miles.

Then I walk a while without talking, and when I do it's to both of them.

"Here's how we come in at the gate. Odo, you're the carter you've always been, a day late with a reason. Corporal Strake asks, you tell her — all of it, the ditch, the fire, the bone, the thirty gold cut for a lieutenant at Wyrm's Rock. Don't soften that last part. Say the words 'Wyrm's Rock' plain and then stop talking and let her write." I glance at him. "I want to see what her pen does when it hears them. A corporal who writes every cart into a book has a book that could tell us how many carters on this road came home and how many didn't. I'd like to be the sort of man she lets read it, and the first step is being the man standing quietly behind an honest carter while he tells the truth.

"Tamsin — you're what you are. A porter who came south with a traveller. If anyone asks what I did, I found a cart in the road and paid a toll. That's true, and it's dull, and dull is what I want to be tonight. The sour fat man stays in the ditch."

And then, because it's been sitting under my cloak since the bridge: "Odo — twenty years on this road. Did you ever hear tell, back in spring, of a woman going south on foot, alone, no money? Paid Ushkar's toll with a coin instead of gold. He kept it. He still looks at it like it owes him an answer."
turns.reply:
James pulls a torch from the pack on Tamsin's back and holds it while she works the tinderbox. She strikes three times. The third spark catches the tow, and the pitch takes with a soft *whump* and a smell like a shipyard. He wedges the torch into the tail-hook, angled down and back, and knocks the worst of the flare off against the cart's iron. A torch won't burn low the way a lamp will, but tipped like that it gives a small, steady circle: the tailboard, the salt sacks under their canvas, the ruts, and Pip's eyes going green for a moment when he looks back at it.

"Honest fire," Tamsin says, putting the tinderbox away. "There. Now we're a cart."

For a while nobody talks. The road climbs, the mule's harness creaks, and the sea keeps up its noise somewhere off to the right.

When James sets out how they'll come in at the gate, Odo walks and listens with his hand on the headstall. At *Wyrm's Rock* his mouth goes tight, as if the words tasted of the camp.

"Tell it and stop," he says. "I can tell it." He walks a few more steps. "Stopping's the hard part. You've heard me. Somebody unties me, I don't shut up." He shakes his head. "I'll say *Wyrm's Rock*. Then I'll look at the mule."

Tamsin hears her own part through and nods at the road ahead.

"Porter. Came south with a traveller. You found a cart and paid a toll." She shrugs the pack higher. "Dull. I've been dull on the quay six years, I'm good at it. Nobody looks twice at the one carrying the box." She doesn't look at him when she says the next bit. "The fat man can stay in the ditch. I'll miss him a bit, though."

Then James asks about the woman. Odo doesn't answer straight away. He frowns at the dark past the torchlight, the way a man counts back over a season of loads.

"Lot of folk on foot in spring," he says. "Pilgrims. Hands looking for work. Mostly they go in twos and threes." He rubs his stubble. "One, though. On her own. Early, before the Greengrass fair. Up near the Gate end, going south. Grey hood, good boots, a stick. No pack to speak of. I said she could ride the tailboard and she said no, thank you, she'd rather walk it." He thinks. "Asked me was the road quiet. I said it was. Back then it was. Nobody'd been took yet."

He's quiet for a few steps.

"She thanked me like I'd given her something. That's why I remember her." He shrugs. "Never saw her come back north. Wouldn't have, mind. Folk go south and I don't count them back."

Tamsin has gone quiet too. When she does speak it's lighter than it needs to be.

"The caravans in spring, then. Same time. You'd have seen them go out. The big ones, off Gray Harbor." She says it to the mule's ears. "Not that it matters. Just, you'd remember them, wouldn't you. Being on the road."

Odo glances at her across the mule's neck. "Saw three, four. Gray Harbor, Little Calimshan. Don't know one from another. Wagons and guards." He waits to see if she'll ask anything else. She doesn't.

"Well," she says, "that's me told," and starts complaining about the weight of the pack. The pack weighs what it weighed an hour ago.

The torch burns down over the next long stretch. The road keeps climbing, then levels out, and the wind drops as the land rises between the road and the sea. It's a little more than an hour before Pip lifts his head beside the wheel and sends something down the bond: *Many. Horses. Meat cooking. Smoke from chimneys, not a camp.*

Then James can see it himself. On the rise ahead a dark mass of old wall stands against the stars, square and heavy, with a tower at one corner and yellow windows high up in it. Below the wall a lantern hangs by the gate. In its light there's a figure on a stool at a little table under an awning, bent over something flat and pale.

The torch on the tail-hook is down to its last hand's width of pitch. The gate is a few hundred feet up the road.

turns.message:
I pull a fresh torch from Tamsin's pack and light it off the stub before it dies, swap them in the tail-hook, and grind the old one out under my boot. Honest carters don't arrive in the dark.

Then I shift the rod to my belt, where it reads as nothing much, and fall in behind the cart on the off side — the traveller walking with the salt, not the man leading it. The crossbow I take back from Tamsin and sling across my own shoulder, unloaded, the bolt back in the quiver. A porter with a loaded crossbow is a question; a traveller with a slung one is furniture.

"Odo, she's yours," I say low. "Walk her up to the table like you've done a hundred times. Day late, with a reason. Tell it, say the words, look at the mule."

I keep a little behind and to the side where the gate lantern falls on Odo and the sacks and only half on me, and I watch Corporal Strake's hands — the pen, the page, whether she turns back to find his name from last month or writes him fresh — and I say nothing at all unless she asks me something directly.

To Pip, down the bond: *stay with the wheel. You're a cart cat.*
turns.reply:
James pulls a fresh torch from the pack on Tamsin's back. He holds it to the guttering stub until the pitch catches, then swaps the new one into the tail-hook and grinds the old one out on the road under his heel. The new flame is taller and brighter for its first minute. It lights the canvas, the black-winged brand on the sacks and the mule's flicking ears.

He holds out his hand for the crossbow. Tamsin gives it up quickly, the way she'd hand back someone else's baby. He works the bolt out of the groove, drops it into the quiver on his belt, eases the string down and slings the bow across his back. The rod goes into his belt. In the torchlight it could be a tent peg.

"Furniture," Tamsin murmurs, as if she's saying it to fix it in her head. She settles the pack and lets her face go dull.

Odo hears his orders with his eyes on the ruts and nods once. *Cart cat,* James sends down the bond. Pip answers by jumping onto the tailboard and arranging himself on the nearest salt sack as if he paid rent on it.

They go up the last few hundred feet at a carter's pace.

The gate stands in a deep arch cut through the old keep wall, and the gate itself is shut. A small postern beside it stands open, with yellow light and noise coming through: talk, a fiddle being tuned badly, a dog. The table under the awning sits to one side, where the lantern falls on it. The woman on the stool is about forty. Her red Fist tabard is faded to brick over a mail shirt, and her hair is cropped short. A shortsword hangs from her belt and a cudgel leans against the table leg. The book in front of her is a thick ledger in a cracked leather cover, open about a third of the way through, with a pen and a horn inkpot beside it. She has looked up long before they reach her.

Odo stops the mule at the table, the way he must have done a hundred times.

"Fennick," the corporal says. It isn't a question. She doesn't write yet. She licks a thumb and turns pages back, a good many, steadily, until she finds what she wants and lays her finger on a line. "Salt, Blackwing, twelve sacks, northbound to the Gate, Tenthday last." Her eyes go to the canvas. "You were due here yesterday noon. You're short."

"Aye, Corporal." Odo takes his cap off. He looks at the ground until he has something to say, then looks up. "Took at the stone bridge yesterday. Orcs. They put her in the ditch and walked me into the trees. Fed me. Never tied me. Took four sacks off the back." He swallows. "Left a bone on the seat for whoever came along. My name, thirty gold, and *Wyrm's Rock*. And under that *LT*."

He stops. He looks at the mule.

The corporal's pen had been moving across the bottom of last month's page. At *Wyrm's Rock* it stops in mid-stroke and stays there.

James is half in the lantern light and half out of it, and from there he can see her hands. They don't shake and they don't hurry. The left hand is still on the page with one finger on Odo's line from last month. The right lays the pen down flat, with the nib off the paper so it won't blot. Then she turns the pages forward again, slower this time, and James gets a glimpse of the month between, line after line of carts in a small square hand. Beside a few of the lines there's a mark in the left margin, made in the same ink as the rest. It's a short slanted tick with a single figure after it. He sees four or five of them before she reaches tonight's page, and two figures that he's sure of: a *2* and a *3*.

She finds the clean line and dips the pen. *Fennick. Salt, Blackwing. 8 sacks.* She writes it neatly. Then she brings the pen down to the margin, makes a short slanted tick, and stops with the nib over the space where the figure should go.

"And that would've been the end of it for three days," she says, to the page. "Bone goes north, your sister finds thirty from somewhere, the Rock pays, and you walk out at the bridge." She looks up at Odo. "Except here you are tonight. So who paid?"

Odo opens his mouth. "There was bread," he begins, "town bread, a proper—" He hears himself and shuts his mouth. He tilts his head back at the off side of the cart without looking round. "He did. Twenty. Straight into the big one's hand, on the road. Never went near the Rock."

Pip yawns on the salt sack.

Corporal Strake lifts the pen off the margin with nothing written after the tick. She looks past the mule's head at the traveller standing half in her light: grey cloak with an old regimental patch, a crossbow slung and unloaded, something wooden at his belt, soft boots. She takes him in from top to bottom without hurrying, as she would a cart.

"You," she says. "Name. And why does a man walking to the Arm pay an orc twenty gold for a carter he's never met, when the Fist would've paid thirty for him?"

turns.message:
I step the rest of the way into the lantern light so she can see all of me, and take my hand well away from the rod at my belt before I speak. I don't take the cap off — I'm not a carter — but I stand the way you stand in front of a corporal who's writing things down, because I was infantry once and the body remembers.

"James Worgen. Late of Queen Zaranda's foot, in Tethyr, scouts after that. Walking to the Arm for work, same as half the men inside." I nod at the cart. "I found it standing in the road an hour before the bridge, with the mule grazing and the bone on the seat. I counted the prints and I counted the sacks, and I did the sum you just did — three days, a sister in Rivington selling her bed, and thirty gold landing in a pocket at Wyrm's Rock that nobody's name is on. I didn't like the sum. I had twenty, the orc wanted a deal more than he wanted a fortress, and the carter was a mile away through the trees. So I paid it."

I let that stand, then add the part she's really asking. "Why not leave it to the Fist? Corporal, I've carried a pay slip for an army. I know what a lieutenant earns. Thirty gold a carter, every one coming home neat in three days, with new silver nobody's spent — that's not a soldier's toll. That's somebody wearing a rank like I wore a fat man's face tonight." I glance at the margin of her book, at the slanted tick with no figure after it, then back to her eyes. "You write every cart in. You know how many of those ticks there've been since spring better than anyone on this road. I'd be glad to tell you everything the orc told me, in order, with no bread in it — and gladder if you'd tell me what number usually goes after that mark."
turns.reply:
James steps the rest of the way into the lantern light. He keeps his hand well clear of the rod and stands the way a man stands in front of a corporal with a pen. His heels come together a little and his chin comes up without him meaning it to. Strake sees it. Her eyes go to the regimental patch on his shoulder and stay there a moment.

She lets him talk all the way through. When he names Queen Zaranda's foot, her mouth moves very slightly. When he says *somebody wearing a rank like I wore a fat man's face tonight*, her eyes come up off the patch and fix on his face, as if checking whether this one is real. Then he looks down at the margin of her book, at the slanted tick with nothing after it, and she sees him do it. Her left hand moves an inch and lies flat across the margin.

She gives him the answer. It isn't his manner that gets it. It's that he did the sum she has been doing alone since spring, out loud, in front of her book, and got the same total.

She keeps her hand on the margin, but she stops covering it and starts using it to point. One square fingertip taps the tick on tonight's line.

"Days," she says. "Bone goes north. Ransom comes back paid. The figure is how many days it took." She turns two pages back with her thumb, finds a line and touches the margin without letting him read the rest of the page. "Two." Another page. "Three. Two. Three." She closes the book on her finger to keep the place. "Since Greengrass. Never a four. I've sent a request for road relief up to the Seatower on a broken axle and waited a month for it."

She looks at Odo, who is staring very hard at the mule, then back at James.

"Fennick gets a tick. No figure. Because the Rock never paid. You did." She says it like reading back a line. "That's the first blank I've had."

She picks the pen up, wipes the nib on a rag and lays it down again, flat, without writing.

"I'll have it in order. All of it. What he said, how he said it, the silver, the rider. Not here." She tips her head a quarter-inch toward the open postern, the fiddle and the noise. "Half that room drives this road and the other half drinks with the ones who do. I'm relieved at the bell. Tap room, the corner bench under the stair. You'll know it, it's the one with nobody on it."

Then she looks at him the way she looked at the cart, slowly and top to bottom, and comes back to his face.

"And the fat man's face. That was a spell." It isn't a question. "I'll want to know whose face you're wearing when you sit down."

She opens the book and writes beside the blank tick, in her small square hand, *paid on road — J. Worgen, 20*. She turns the ledger round a few degrees so Odo can see it.

"Fennick. Kitchen door's round the side. Margery's been asking after her salt since noon." Her eyes come back to the traveller. "Worgen. Postern's open."

Behind James, Tamsin lets out a breath, very quietly.

"Mine," I say. "When I sit down it'll be the one you're looking at now. The other one's in a ditch by the brook and he isn't coming out." I give her the nod a soldier gives a corporal — not a salute, I'm not hers — and step back out of her light.

"Corner bench under the stair, at the bell. I'll be the one on it."

Then, to Odo, low as the cart starts to roll toward the side of the keep: "Kitchen. Tell Margery Thorne the salt's a day late because of orcs and the carter's whole because of nobody in particular. If she asks who paid, say a traveller, and let her come and find me if she wants the rest." I put a hand on the mule's neck a moment where his has been all day. "Go on. You're early."

And to Tamsin, as we go in through the postern and the fiddle and the dog-smell and the heat of a common room hit us like a wall: "Dull. Find us the corner bench and sit on it like you own it. I'll get us bread and whatever they're pouring, and we'll see who in this room looks up when a Blackwing cart comes in a day late with a strange man walking beside it."

I let Pip jump down and go wherever a cart cat goes, and I walk to the bar.
turns.reply:
Strake hears him out. When he says *the one you're looking at now*, she looks at that face for a moment longer, the way she checks a load against its line. Then she nods once and goes back to her book. As he steps out of the lantern light the pen starts moving again, and she's writing something that isn't about Odo's sacks.

Odo takes the message for Margery and moves his lips over it once, *orcs, nobody in particular, a traveller*, the way he'd go over a delivery note. When James's hand goes to the mule's neck the carter watches it. He doesn't say anything. He clicks his tongue and the cart creaks off along the wall toward the side of the keep, with the torch on the tail-hook bobbing away into the dark. Pip waits until the wheels are turning, then drops off the salt sack and goes after the smell of the kitchen with his tail straight up.

Then the postern, and the heat.

The tap room is low and wide under smoke-black beams, and it's full. Carters sit in their shirtsleeves. A table of caravan guards still has their mail on and is dicing for the next round. Two pilgrims in grey are asleep sitting up. By the hearth a big brindle mastiff lies on its side, taking up most of the floor. On a stool near the stair, the fiddler has given up tuning and is just playing, a little flat. The air smells of mutton, wet wool and ale spilled on old wood.

A few heads come up at the door, the way heads always do: two carters, one guard. They look him over, cloak, slung crossbow, soft boots, and go back to their cups. Nobody looks for long. He's a man off the road, and the room is full of those.

There's one exception. At a table by the hearth four people are playing cards. The dealer is lean and clean-shaven, in a good dark coat that's too good for the room. He looks up at the postern before anyone else does, and he looks down again first. Before each deal he squares the deck with his thumb run along the bottom edge, neat and unhurried, every time. Across from him sits a woman of about fifty, short and thick through the arms, with a brown shawl and a small cloth purse on the table in front of her. She frowns at her hand as if it had said something rude.

Tamsin walks past all of it to the stair. The corner bench under it is empty, as promised. She drops the pack on one end, sits on the other, and puts her boots up on the pack. Now it's her bench, and she makes sure the room can see that.

At the back of James's head comes Pip, far off and pleased with himself: *Meat. Warm. Woman with a big spoon.* Then, sharper: *Dog. Big. Stupid. Asleep.*

The barman is a lad of about twenty with flour on one sleeve and the beginnings of a moustache he's clearly proud of. He's talking before James reaches the bar.

"Evening, evening. Off the road? You've got the road all over you." He's already wiping a mug that doesn't need wiping. "Stew's mutton, three copper with bread, and the bread's today's, I'll swear to it. Ale's four, cider's four, the good cider's six and it isn't really better, don't tell anyone." He leans in, cheerful. "Came up the Way? From the Gate? You'll have come over the stone bridge, then." His eyes light up. "Everyone's got a story about that bridge. What's yours?"

 *(Out of game: none of these needed a roll.)*

1. **Odo and the message:** that happened as you said it. Odo went over the message for Margery once under his breath and took it round to the kitchen.
2. **Sending the cart off:** that happened too. Odo watched your hand on the mule's neck, said nothing, clicked his tongue, and the cart creaked off toward the side of the keep.
3. **Tamsin and the bench:** done. She's on the corner bench under the stair with her boots up on the pack, and anyone looking can see it's hers.
4. **Bread and drink:** this one isn't done yet, because Fenwick has given you prices and asked for your story, and the coin is yours to spend. Mutton stew with bread is three copper a bowl. Ale or cider is four a mug, and the good cider is six. Tell me what you order and pay for, and I'll put it on the bench.

I put a silver on the bar, which is more than two stews and two ales come to, and don't ask for the change back yet.

"Two of the mutton, two of the plain ale. The good cider can stay a secret." I keep my voice easy and a little tired, the voice of a man with nothing to tell. "My bridge story's the dullest one you'll hear tonight, lad. Found a salt cart in the road with its mule grazing. Walked it down to the bridge. Three orcs wanted a toll. I paid it, they let us by. That's the whole of it." I shrug. "Carter's round at your kitchen door now, if Margery wants it from him. He tells it better. He was there longer."

I let him see me not looking at the card table — which takes doing, because I've already seen it. The thumb along the bottom edge before every deal: a man who wants to know where the last card sits. I've done it myself, years back, on worse nights than this. The Lady's coin lies quiet against my chest, and I keep it that way by turning my shoulder to the hearth.

"One thing, since you're the man who knows the room." I tip my head a bare inch toward the fire without turning. "The coat by the hearth. Too good for mutton stew. Is he a regular, or did he come off the road like me?"

Then I take the two bowls and the mugs when they come, and carry them to the bench under the stair.
turns.reply:
James sets a silver piece on the bar and leaves his hand off it. Fenwick's eyes go to the coin, then to James's face. He looks like he's waiting for the story to start properly.

The story is all there is. Fenwick listens to the cart, the bridge, the toll and the letting by. By the end his moustache has drooped a little.

"That's it? You *paid* it?" He sounds like a man whose pie turned out to have no filling. "Last week a drover told me he fought off six of them with a pitchfork. I mean, he was lying, his pitchfork was in the cart the whole time, but still." Then he hears *the carter's round at your kitchen door*, and he brightens and glances at the hatch behind him, where steam and a woman's voice are coming through. "Oh, Margery'll have that out of him before the bread's cut."

He picks up the silver, looks at it, and holds up his other hand with the fingers spread.

"Two mutton, two plain, that's fourteen copper, sir. This is ten." He doesn't say it unkindly. "Bring me the four when you've eaten. You've an honest face. Your *own* face, anyway." He laughs at that himself and turns to ladle the stew.

He doesn't turn round to answer the question about the coat, and he doesn't drop his voice. Fenwick doesn't seem to know there is any other way to talk. "Not a regular. Came up from the Gate this afternoon on a hired grey, took the room over the stable and the table by the fire, and he's been dealing since the lamps went up. Master Morrow. Says wine, going south to Beregost." Two bowls slop onto the board, then two mugs. "Wins more than he loses, but not so much anyone's thrown a chair yet. Tips in silver." He wipes his hands. "The lady across from him's been losing to him since supper. Came up on the Rivington carrier this morning. She's been at this bar twice asking has anyone come up past the stone bridge today." He looks at James with honest interest. "You have."

James takes the bowls in one hand and the two mugs by their handles in the other. He keeps his shoulder to the hearth and carries them across to the stair.

Tamsin takes her bowl without taking her boots off the pack. She's sitting with her back to the wall and can see the whole room, and her eyes don't move much while she eats.

"Coat looked over here twice while you were at the bar," she says round a mouthful of mutton. "At you. Not me. Nobody looks at the porter, I told you." She blows on the next spoonful. "And the shawl's opened that little purse again. That's three times since we sat down. On the quay, when a woman keeps going back to the same purse, it's because she's counting what's left in it."

The fiddler finds the right note at last, holds it a moment, and loses it again.

*(Out of game: two stews and two ales come to fourteen copper and a silver is ten, so there's no change. Fenwick has let you owe him the other four.)*

I eat three spoonfuls standing, because a man who's walked from the Gate eats, and then I set the bowl down.

"Tamsin. Four copper for Fenwick, and then round to the kitchen door. Find Odo. Tell him there's a woman in a brown shawl in the tap room who came up from Rivington this morning and has been asking all day whether anyone's come past the stone bridge. Tell him to come and see her face before he says anything else to Margery. Don't say the name — let him say it."

I dig the coppers out and put them in her hand, and I wait until she's through the hatch door before I move.

Then I go to the hearth. Not to the table — to the woman's chair. I stand behind her shoulder where she has to turn to see me and the dealer has to look up past her, and I keep both hands in plain sight, well away from the cards and my own belt. I don't look at Master Morrow's deck, though it costs me something not to.

"Mistress," I say, low enough for her and no lower. "The lad at the bar says you've been asking after the stone bridge. I came over it tonight. There was a salt cart in the road with Blackwing's mark on the sacks, and a carter leading it who'd been a day late for a bad reason and is whole for a good one. He's round at the kitchen door now." I nod at the purse on the table in front of her, once, not touching it. "I'd close that and come and see him before you put anything else on the cloth. Whatever you came down with, I think you'll find you don't need it tonight."
turns.reply:
James takes three spoonfuls of the stew standing up, the way a man eats who has walked from the Gate. It's hot and salty, with more barley than mutton. He puts the bowl down on the bench by Tamsin's boots.

Tamsin listens with the spoon halfway to her mouth. At *a woman in a brown shawl* her eyes go to the hearth. By *Rivington* she has put the spoon back in the bowl.

"Oh," she says quietly. "Oh, *that's* why she keeps counting." She takes the four coppers out of his palm and gets her boots off the pack in one movement. "Don't say the name. Let him say it. Right."

At the bar she slaps the coppers down in front of Fenwick. "Four, from the honest face." Before he can start talking she's pointing at the door beside the hatch, where the steam is coming through. He lifts the bar flap for her with a grin, and she goes into the kitchen noise. The door swings shut behind her.

Then James goes to the hearth.

The mastiff lifts one eyelid as he steps over its tail and lets it drop again. The card table is close to the fire and the cloth is scorched brown along one edge. The game is Three-Dragon Ante, the painted dragon cards worn soft at the corners. Sitting in are a young drover with his sleeves rolled, an old man with a cold pipe in his teeth, the woman in the brown shawl, and Master Morrow. There's a small heap of coin in the middle of the cloth, mostly silver, with a few gold pieces on top.

James stops behind the woman's chair, at her shoulder. She has to turn her head to see him, and the dealer has to look up past her. He keeps his hands in plain sight and his eyes off the deck.

Morrow looks up first, the same as at the postern. This time he doesn't look down again. He just waits, courteous, with the deck squared under his hand.

The woman turns. Up close she has a broad, weathered face and grey hair scraped back hard, with forearms like a laundress's. She hears *salt cart* without moving. At *Blackwing's mark* her hand closes flat over the little purse. At *whole for a good one* the breath goes out of her all at once, as if someone had stepped off her chest.

"Odo," she says. It isn't loud. The old man with the pipe takes it out of his mouth. "That's my brother. Short, grey, boots gone at the heels, never late in his life." She's already pushing her chair back. Her cards are still fanned in her other fist and she's forgotten them. "Round the kitchen, you said. He's *here*."

"Then that's good news, and I'm glad for you, mistress." Morrow's voice is low and pleasant. He doesn't raise it to carry. He lays the deck down and rests two fingers beside it on the cloth. "Only the hand's dealt, and your six are in the pot." He tips his head at the gold on top of the heap. "Fold, and they stay where they are. That's the cloth, not me. Play it out, and they may go home with you." He lifts his eyes past her shoulder to James and smiles a little. "Your friend's welcome to stand and watch. The table doesn't mind an audience."

The drover looks from the pot to the woman and back again, plainly hoping she'll fold.

At the back of James's head, far off and sudden, comes Pip: *Girl here. Loud. The man stands up fast. Spoon drops.*

The woman is half out of her chair with the purse in one hand and her cards in the other. She looks at the six gold on the heap. It's money she brought south for a ransom, and she has been losing it since supper. She looks at the kitchen door. Then she looks up at James, because he's the one who brought the news.

"You saw him," she says. "With your own eyes. He's not hurt?"

turns.message:
"With my own eyes, mistress. Not a mark on him. They fed him town bread and never tied his hands, and the only thing he's sore about is that someone else put his cart in a ditch." I keep my voice where it was. "He's standing in Margery Thorne's kitchen right now dropping spoons because a porter just told him his sister's out here. Go."

She looks at the six gold on the heap, and I see what Tamsin saw — a woman counting what's left.

"Put the cards face down on the cloth and leave them there," I tell her, quiet. "Six gold is a hard thing to leave. A bed sold out from under you to pay a lieutenant who never earned it is harder, and you came down this road ready to do that. You don't have to now. Take the purse to your brother. That's the better hand."

Then I look up at Master Morrow for the first time, and I look at his face and not his thumb — which costs me, and he may see that it does. I don't touch the table.

"The cloth says fold and they stay. I know the cloth. But the table's four people and a dealer, not a cloth." I let my eyes go to the drover and the old man with the pipe. "A woman's brother came home from an orc camp tonight and she's leaving to see him. Any man here who'd rather take her ransom money than let the hand stand dead and the pot go back where it came from — he can say so, and we'll all know it about him. Myself, I'd call the hand spoiled and deal again." I give Morrow a small, civil nod, dealer to a man who's held a deck. "Your call, Master Morrow. I'm only watching."
turns.reply:
"With my own eyes," Wenna says under her breath, and stops there. She asked it twice, and she got her answer twice.

She looks at the six gold on the heap a moment longer. Then she does what he told her. She lays her fan of dragons face down on the scorched cloth, squares it with the flat of her hand, and keeps the purse closed in her other fist.

Then James looks up at Master Morrow, at his face and not his hands, and talks to the whole table.

Nobody at the table answers right away.

The old man with the cold pipe answers first. He takes the pipe out of his mouth, taps the stem twice on the cloth beside his own cards, and turns them face down.

"Dead hand," he says. "Her brother's home. I'll not win off that." He doesn't look at Morrow when he says it. He looks at the drover.

The drover goes red to the ears. He'd been counting that pot as his. Now every carter in earshot has turned round on the bench to watch the hearth table, and the guards' dice have stopped. He mutters something about it being a good hand, and then he puts it face down too, quickly, like dropping a coal.

That leaves the dealer. The room is watching him now, not the stranger, and a man who wants to go unremembered can't stand being looked at like that. Master Morrow gives way without a fight. He takes his time and makes it look gracious.

"Spoiled, then." He says it lightly, as though he had been about to suggest it himself. With two fingers he separates the six gold from the top of the heap and slides them across the cloth to Wenna, then sorts the silver back by the order it went in. He does it from memory and gets it exactly right. "Every man his own stake. Mistress, I'm glad for your brother."

Wenna sweeps the six into her purse without counting them. She knows how many there are. She jerks the cord tight, and for a moment her broad face doesn't seem to know what to do with itself.

The kitchen door bangs open beside the hatch.

Odo comes through it with his cap in his fist and gravy on his jerkin. Tamsin is a step behind him. He's moving faster than he moved all the way up from the bridge. He stops at the edge of the hearth light, and Wenna is already round the table.

She doesn't embrace him. She takes him by both arms above the elbows and looks him over hard from his stubble to his boots, the way she'd look over a cart she was thinking of buying.

"Not a mark," she says. "He said not a mark." Then she cuffs him once on the shoulder, not gently. "A *day*, Odo."

"Weren't me," Odo says hoarsely. "They put her in the ditch, Wen, I never—" She cuffs him again, and he stops, and she keeps hold of his sleeve.

Fenwick has come halfway down the bar with a mug he isn't wiping, hoping for the story at last. Tamsin edges round the pair of them toward the stair. As she passes James she gives him a look that is pure quay: *well, that's one bill settled.*

turns.message:
I look at the empty chair for a long moment. I know exactly what it would feel like to sit in it — the warmth of the fire on my left, the weight of the painted dragons in my hand, the old quiet that comes when the only thing in the world is the next card. The coin on my chest stays warm and says nothing, and that's worse than if it had burned.

"I've held one," I say. "I put it down." I rest my fingertips on the back of the chair, lightly, and take them off again. "There's a man I owe a hearing to tonight and a corporal who'll want my face where she can see it, so the chairs can go to someone who still plays."

Then, because he asked a question with that offer and I'd rather answer it with one: "You came up from the Gate today on a hired grey, the lad says. Wine, south to Beregost." I nod at the room, the carters, the ledger outside the gate. "It's a bad month to be a man alone on this road with gold enough to tip in silver, Master Morrow. The orcs at the bridge take tolls and the Rock takes the rest. I'd ride out early, in company, and I'd keep the deck in your coat where the Fist can't see you square it."

I give him the same small civil nod I gave him before, and go back to the bench under the stair to wait for the bell.
turns.reply:
James looks at the empty chair for a while. The fire is warm on that side, and the painted dragons lie face down on the scorched cloth, soft at the corners. Morrow watches him look and says nothing. He knows when to let a man look.

Then the fingertips touch the chair-back and lift away again, and Morrow's face stays exactly as courteous as it was.

"Put it down," he says, as if he were noting a price. "Few manage that. Fewer say so out loud." He hears the rest out with his hands flat on the cloth: the hired grey, the wine, the bad month, the bridge and the Rock. At *where the Fist can't see you square it* nothing moves in his face. But he picks the deck up off the middle of the cloth and slides it into the inside pocket of the good dark coat in one movement. He doesn't square it first.

"Sound advice." His voice is low and pleasant, pitched under the fiddle. "Early, and in company. I'll take it." He lets a moment pass. "You seem to know the road's arrangements better than a man who came up it this evening ought to. I'll remember that, Master..." He leaves the space open. When it stays empty he smiles slightly, as if that were an answer too, and lifts two fingers to Fenwick for wine.

James gives him the small civil nod and walks back across the room. He steps over the mastiff's tail again, and this time the dog doesn't bother to open an eye.

Tamsin has her boots back up on the pack. She waits until he's sitting down, then speaks to her stew.

"You told him." She chases a lump of barley round the bowl. "Didn't say what, didn't say how. Just *I saw*, and walked off. Harbourmaster does that to the Calishite captains. Leaves them up all night wondering which bit he means." She finally gets the barley. "The coat's not looking at you now. He's looking at the door. Twice already."

James's bowl is where he left it, gone lukewarm. Before he can get to it, a shadow falls across the bench.

It's Wenna, with Odo behind her. She still has him by the sleeve, and he's let himself be towed the way a mule lets itself be led to water. Up close she smells of the Rivington carrier, horse and damp wool. She looks at James the way she looked her brother over: plainly, from his boots up, as if checking a delivery against a docket.

"Odo says twenty," she says. "Gold. Into the big one's hand, out of your own purse. He says you wore a fat man's face to do it." She doesn't seem to think the face is the strange part. Her free hand comes out from under the shawl with the little cloth purse in it, and she sets it on the bench beside his stew. It clinks heavily. "Six. That's what come back off the table. The rest by Midwinter, off the salt. I don't take what I can't pay." Her jaw is set. "And you'll eat with us in Rivington when you're back in the Gate. He says you'll say no. I'm not asking."

Odo stands behind her looking at the floor. His cap is twisting in his hands. He doesn't say anything, but he doesn't look like he'll argue with her either.

The purse sits on the bench between the stew and Tamsin's boots, tied shut, waiting for James to take it or turn it down.

turns.message:
I don't pick the purse up straight away. I look at her, and then at Odo twisting his cap, and I understand that pushing it back across the bench would be the one unkindness I could do her tonight.

So I untie it, count six gold out onto my palm so she can see I've counted, and close my hand on them.

"Six," I say. "Taken, and the slate's clean. There's no rest by Midwinter — that's not me letting you off, mistress, it's me telling you what the price was. The orc wanted twenty. Fourteen of that was the Lady's business and six was yours, and now you've paid yours." I tuck the coins away and hand her back the empty purse, tied. "The salt goes to the Arm's kitchen and the bed stays in Rivington. That's the deal I want."

Then I look at Odo. "And I'll eat with you in Rivington. I've been told she doesn't hear no, so I won't waste one."

I nod toward the kitchen door, low. "Go and get fed before Margery gives your bowl to the cat — he's already found her spoon. The corporal's bell's soon, and I'll be sitting right here when it rings."
turns.reply:
Wenna watches him untie the cord. She watches each coin come out onto his palm, one, two, up to six, the way she'd watch a man weigh her flour. When he closes his hand on them she lets out a short breath through her nose.

She hears the rest with her jaw set. At *the Lady's business* her eyes drop to his chest, where the grey cloak hangs over something on a cord, and then come back up to his face.

"I don't know your Lady," she says. "Never had dealings with her." She takes the empty purse back and holds it a moment. It's light now, and she knows it. "But I heard the price. Six." Her mouth works. Wenna Fennick doesn't say things she doesn't mean, so she doesn't say much. "Thank you."

She pushes the purse into her shawl and turns half round to her brother. "He'll eat with us."

"Told you he'd say no," Odo says hoarsely.

"He never said no." She cuffs him on the shoulder again, more lightly this time, mostly to keep her hand busy. To James: "Rope Street, behind the tannery yard. Blue door, it's the only one. Ask for Wenna, they'll point." Then she sees him nod at the kitchen door. She takes Odo by the sleeve again and steers him off through the room, past the mastiff and the carters, the way she'd steer a cart through a narrow gate. Odo looks back once from the hatch door, cap in his fist. He doesn't say anything. Then the door swings and the kitchen noise swallows them both.

At the back of James's head, faint and warm: *Spoon woman. Loud. Gives me fat.*

Tamsin waits until the door has stopped swinging. She's been working on the same crust for a while.

"Fourteen to the Lady," she says to the crust. "Does she write you a docket for that, or do you just have to trust her?" She glances at him sideways, then back at the room. "Coat's wine came. He hasn't touched it. He's watching the postern."

By the hearth Master Morrow sits with a full cup at his elbow, the deck put away and his hands flat on the scorched cloth. The fiddler starts something slower. Out past the postern there's no bell yet. It's about twenty minutes off, and nothing else happens before it rings unless you want it to.

turns.message:
I pull the lukewarm bowl toward me and eat properly this time, because the next hour is going to be talking.

"No docket," I tell the stew. "She doesn't write anything down. That's the whole trouble with her — you put it on the table and you find out afterward what it cost." I break the bread. "Fourteen gold for a carter walking home early is the cheapest she's ever charged me. I'll take it and not ask for a receipt."

I don't look at the hearth. I watch Morrow in the dull side of my ale mug instead — a man who's put his cards away, left good wine standing, and is counting how many times the postern opens. That's not a man resting before an early start. That's a man who's expecting someone off the road tonight, and would rather it looked like he wasn't.

"Tamsin. One more dull errand, and then you can sit for the rest of the night. Go out past the postern like you're checking the pack's straps on the cart — Odo left it by the wall. Look in the stable on your way back. I want to know about his hired grey: is it unsaddled and bedded down for the night, or is it standing ready? And how many other horses are in there that came in today." I wipe the bowl with the bread. "Don't talk to anyone. Come back and sit down and tell me with your mouth full, like it's gossip."

And one quiet thing, as she stands: "And the caravans off Gray Harbor in spring. You asked Odo like it didn't matter. When you want to tell me why it does, I'll listen. Not before."
turns.reply:
James pulls the bowl over and eats it properly this time. It's gone past lukewarm toward cold, and the barley has thickened into something you could build a wall with. He eats it anyway, like a man who knows what the next hour holds.

Tamsin hears the answer about the docket without looking at him. She turns the last of her crust over in her fingers.

"No receipt," she says. "Harbourmaster'd have a fit." She chews. "On the quay that's what you call a tab. Nobody likes a tab. You never know what you're up to on it till the man says."

The ale mug is pewter, dented and dull. Tilted on the bench at the right angle, its side gives James a smeared, curved picture of the hearth: a blot of dark coat, a pale face, and the pale square of the cup standing full beside it. That's not enough to read a man by. It is enough to see the coat shift each time cold air comes through the postern. A carter goes out to piss, and the coat shifts. The carter comes back, and it shifts again, then settles.

Tamsin listens to the errand with her eyes on the room.

"Pack's under my boots," she says out of the corner of her mouth. "Not on the cart. You're tired." She doesn't make anything of it. "I'll say I'm seeing Odo's mule got its water. Nobody asks a porter why she's looking at a mule." Under her breath: "Grey. Saddled or bedded. How many in today. Don't talk." She swings her boots down off the pack.

She's halfway up when he says the last thing, quietly.

She stops. For a moment her face isn't doing anything at all. It isn't the quay face or the dull face, and that's rarer on Tamsin than either of them. She looks down at him, then at the postern.

"Noted," she says, the way a clerk says it to close a line. Then she goes.

In the mug's dented side the dark coat turns its head as she crosses the room, and keeps it turned until the postern swings shut behind her.

James finishes the stew and wipes the bowl with the last of the bread. The fiddler gets through the slow tune and starts it again. By the hearth the old man has his pipe lit at last and puffs at it, pleased with himself. At the bar the young drover is telling Fenwick that it was a good hand, a *really* good hand. Fenwick says, "I'm sure it was," and wipes a mug at him in sympathy. Through the hatch comes the clatter of a ladle on iron and a woman's voice rising over the kitchen noise, too muffled to make out. It may be Margery Thorne getting the story out of a carter.

Tamsin is gone for about as long as it takes to water a mule. When the postern opens again she comes in rubbing her hands against the cold. In the pewter the dark coat follows her across the room, the way it did when she left. Then, for the first time in a while, it turns toward the corner bench.

She drops back onto her end of the bench, puts her boots up, takes the heel of her own bread off the plate and talks round it, bored, like someone passing on who's sleeping with whom.

"Mule's got water. Odo'd done it already, course he had." She chews. "Stable's down the side, past the kitchen door. Lad's asleep in the straw by the lamp, didn't wake him. Seven horses. Three in today with road mud still wet on the legs, cobs, same brand on the rump as the patch on that lot's sleeves." She tips her chin a hair toward the dicing guards. "Three with dry coats, been there days. And the grey."

She takes another bite before she gives him the rest.

"Grey's bedded. Rubbed down, rug on, hay in the net, the lot. He's not standing ready." She swallows. "But his saddle's not in the tack room with the others. Everybody else's tack is on the pegs inside. His is on his own stall door, bags still buckled to it, bridle hung on the post right by his head. You could have him tacked up in the time it takes to say it." She shrugs. "On the quay, a man who leaves his hook on the cart instead of the hut means to be first on tomorrow's load. Or he just doesn't trust the hut." She licks a crumb off her thumb. "Could be either. He did say early."

In the pewter the pale face is still turned toward the stair. Then it turns away. A hand comes up and lifts the wine, and for the first time since Fenwick poured it, Master Morrow drinks.

Out past the postern the bell hasn't rung yet. It's about ten minutes off, and nothing else happens before then unless you want it to.

 *(Out of game: none of these needed a roll. Eating, talking and watching a reflection carry no risk and have nobody to roll against, and Tamsin's look round the stable was routine work for a porter with only a sleeping stable lad nearby, so the last turn tells them all as they happened.)*
